3130 Greenmount Avenue was the general offices of THE HOOPER FOOD CO., Inc., a Baltimore seafood-restaurant chain. It began with G. Carroll Hooper, a stockbroker ruined by the 1929 crash, who in December 1932 opened a seafood restaurant in a converted one-car garage at 511 Gorsuch Ave in Waverly. 'Hooper's' grew into a small chain: restaurants at 511 Gorsuch Ave, 415 E 32nd St, and 3 W Chesapeake Ave (Towson), plus seafood stores at 3200 Old York Rd and the North Avenue Market - a food business strung right along the York Road/Greenmount spine. Its menus survive in the Enoch Pratt Free Library's 'Maryland Menus' collection (Digital Maryland). Its flagship 511 Gorsuch Ave location later became Eddie & Brooks Robinson's Gorsuch House restaurant (near Memorial Stadium) - so one corner carried a Depression-era seafood chain and, later, an Orioles Hall of Famer's restaurant.

The MSA liquor-license record for 511 Gorsuch gives the establishment's full name-chain: Zipper's; The Port Hole; Gorsuch's House; Robinson's Gorsuch House; Brook Robinson's Gorsuch House Restaurant; Eddie Robinson's Gorsuch House; Hooper's Gorsuch House; Hooper Food Co.; Hooper's Restaurant. Hooper's and the Gorsuch House were the same building.

In December 1932, G. Carroll Hooper — a stockbroker ruined by the 1929 crash — opened a seafood restaurant in a converted one-car garage at 511 Gorsuch Ave. It grew into The Hooper Food Co., a Baltimore seafood-restaurant chain (HQ later given on a menu as 3130 Greenmount, corridor parcel #750), with outlets at 3 W Chesapeake Ave (Towson), 415 E 32nd St, and seafood stores at 3200 Old York Rd and the North Avenue Market.

Two generations later the same 511 Gorsuch building became Eddie Robinson's Gorsuch House, then — after Brooks Robinson bought a partial interest (~1961/64) — 'Eddie and Brooks Robinson's Gorsuch House' ('Robby's crabcakes'). A Baltimore Museum of Industry photo dated Dec 10, 1958 shows the porthole storefront. The restaurant venture was part of the sporting-goods/restaurant portfolio that nearly bankrupted Brooks in the mid-1970s.

2900 Greenmount, the NW corner of 29th directly at Terrapin/Oriole Park's gate, was J. Firman's SALOON (1914-18; 'J Firman saloon 2900 Greenmount av h do', with a live-in bartender) - a ballpark corner tavern. Under Prohibition it pivoted: Firman became manager of the Tompkins malt-supply company next door at 2902, while 2900 itself turned to Greek-run confectioners (Kousonris 1921, Peter & Rosa Lokos 1922-23) and a 'Pleasure Club' social club. The Sanborn shows the corner as 'Hardw./Rest.' A textbook saloon-to-dry-era pivot right at the ballpark gate.

The west (even) side of the 2900 block, between E 29th and E 30th, WAS the ballpark. The 1915 Sanborn (sheet 710, Block 3) labels it 'TERRAPIN PARK - FEDERAL LEAGUE BASEBALL GROUNDS - CLOSED AT TIME OF SURVEY' - an all-FRAME (wood) grandstand ~22 ft high with a main Grand Stand and Pavilions A & B, and a run of OPEN BLEACHERS fronting directly on Greenmount across the mid-block (roughly 2906-2928, where the Polk shows no houses). Built for the Federal League Baltimore Terrapins (1914-15); the Polk lists it as 'Balto Baseball Co / Federal League Baseball Co, Greenmount av c 29th' (1914-15). After the Federal League folded, Jack Dunn's International League Orioles moved in and it became 'Oriole Baseball Park' (Polk, 1918) - the park where the IL Orioles won seven straight pennants (1919-25) and the Negro-NL Elite Giants played (1938-42), until it burned July 3-4, 1944. This parcel (2920) sits on the old bleacher frontage.

A Sept 23 1985 $60,000 purchase-money deed of trust to First National Bank of Maryland (SEB 658/574) also encumbered 902 Sibley Road in the county; a Nov 14 1985 confirmatory agreement (SEB 707/336) corrected the owners' names after their naturalization — Kang Jung Yi became Dandy Kangjung Lee and Kyung Cha Yi became June Kyungcha Lee (the husband adopting the store's own name, 'Dandy'). A 1997 intra-spousal deed put title in June Kyung Cha Lee alone (Liber 658/570), secured by a Korea Exchange Bank indemnity mortgage (Book 6291/113, satisfied 2001, FMC 1889/357). By 2001 she had moved to Allentown, PA; on Dec 30 2003 she and So Cheung Lee refinanced with a $202,500 Wachovia Bank deed of trust (FMC 4871/350), paying off a prior $128,671 balance. The lender succession — First National → Korea Exchange → Wachovia — tracks the corridor's Korean-immigrant merchant thread.

3221 was an investment parcel of Alan Wurtzburger (Apr 22 1900 – Feb 20 1963), a Baltimore commercial real-estate investor who was also one of the museum world's great collectors (BMA Trustee 1955-62). That dual identity resolves why a celebrated art collector held a modest Greenmount storefront: 3221 — and its corner neighbor 3223, which Alan bought out of an estate in 1934 (Emanuel E. Ottenheimer, Executor → Alan Wurtzburger) — were income/rental parcels in his real-estate portfolio, not a shop the family ran. Alan deeded 3221 to his wife Janet E. Cohn Wurtzburger (Jan 29 1908, Cleveland – Dec 24 1973) on June 1 1945 — confirming the 'C.' in the land record's 'Janet E. C. Wurtzburger' is COHN (a German-Jewish surname), not 'Cahn.' On Janet's death the 1976 estate split 3221 between their children Jon Alan Wurtzburger (b.1934; stockbroker, a retired Governor of the New York Stock Exchange, aviator and philanthropist) and Margot 'Peggy' Wurtzburger Milch, who sold it to the Lim family in 1979. (Emanuel E. Ottenheimer was of the Baltimore German-Jewish Ottenheimer publishing family; no Wurtzburger–Ottenheimer kinship is documented — the 1934 deed was a real-estate transaction.)

Alan and Janet Wurtzburger were among the Baltimore Museum of Art's greatest benefactors. In two phases they gave the museum its foundational non-Western holdings — 400+ African, Oceanic, and Pre-Columbian sculptures (major African gift 1954-55; Pre-Columbian core 1958), establishing the Wurtzburger Gallery of the Primitive Arts (1958; catalogued by Paul S. Wingert, 'The Alan Wurtzburger Collection of African Sculpture,' BMA 1958) — and they assembled a landmark modern-sculpture collection: a Rodin (a 'Balzac'), Bourdelle, Maillol, Henry Moore, Jacob Epstein, Marino Marini, Jacques Lipchitz, Ossip Zadkine, Alexander Calder, Isamu Noguchi, and José de Rivera. The sculpture was first displayed on the grounds of their Stevenson (Baltimore County) estate 'Timberlane' (landscaped by James Rose and Thomas Church); the 1.1-acre Alan and Janet Wurtzburger Sculpture Garden opened at the BMA in 1980 (landscape architect George Patton). The Wurtzburgers belong to the same German-Jewish art-collecting-and-philanthropy tradition as Baltimore's Cone sisters.

Tobias Stansbury, whose 1671 land assignment would underlie the 1688 patent for the site's founding tract, arrived in the Maryland colony as an indentured servant.
Stansbury received the land assignment on "Brittains Ridge" that later formed the basis of the 1688 "Huntington and Merryman's Lot" patent.

Lord Baltimore granted the tract "Huntington and Merryman's Lot," on the piedmont then called "Brittains Ridge," to Tobias Stansboro and Charles Merryman -- the founding land grant underlying the corridor that would become the Old Oriole Park wedge.
Thomas Gorsuch constructed the corridor's first recorded residence on the tract.
An estate inventory for Sarah Merryman documented enslaved individuals held on the family's land within the tract's chain of title.
An indenture executed by the Merryman family conveyed an enslaved man named Tom.
A Gilmor family member placed a newspaper advertisement seeking the return of an enslaved man named Ned who had escaped.
An 1799 yellow fever outbreak in Baltimore is noted as affecting households on the estates later comprising the corridor.
Colonel James Biays built the Mt. Jefferson estate directly on the future ballpark wedge; one dossier passage cites a construction date as early as 1780.
James Biays built the road connecting Bond Street to the York Road that would become Greenmount Avenue.
James Biays formed a business partnership with General Samuel Smith, from whom the Mt. Jefferson tract had passed.
A tollgate/tollhouse was built near Gilmore Lane on the road that became Greenmount Avenue.
Samuel Smith, from whom the tract passed to Biays, was documented owning eight enslaved people in 1813.
An 1813 Biays household account references provisioning for a servant, possibly enslaved, on the Mt. Jefferson estate.
Colonel James Biays led a cavalry unit at the Battle of North Point during the War of 1812; Mt. Jefferson served as a cavalry rendezvous point and his troops scouted the British landing.
Two separate foreclosure actions were recorded against James Biays's real-estate holdings, signaling financial strain that preceded the estate's later breakup.
The 1820 federal census recorded both enslaved and free Black residents in the vicinity of the corridor's estates.
Biays, owner of Mt. Jefferson, died July 30, 1822; an active creditor petition against his estate followed almost immediately, reflecting the financial distress documented since 1816.
General Samuel Smith's heirs brought suit against the Biays estate over unresolved debts tied to the Mt. Jefferson tract.
Samuel Smith, an enslaver whose land became part of the corridor, was active in the American Colonization Society.
A manumission record documents the freeing of an enslaved woman named Sarah connected to the corridor's landowning families.
Samuel Brady, later the wedge's namesake 19th-century estate owner, served as Baltimore's city tax collector before his mayoralty.
An enslaved woman named Ann Barnes was manumitted, per a Baltimore County record tied to a corridor landowning family.
The 1840 federal census recorded members of the Gilmor family, tied to the corridor's chain of title, as holders of enslaved people.
Samuel Brady served as 11th Mayor of Baltimore, 1840-1842, while owning the estate that became the ballpark wedge.
An enslaved man named Levi Cosley escaped in October 1840 from a corridor-area household; his body was recovered in January 1841, per a follow-up newspaper report.
Mayor Samuel Brady signed a city ordinance establishing fire hydrants during his term.

Members of the Brady and Sadtler families appear repeatedly in Baltimore newspapers between 1848 and 1878 -- school-board service (1848), a school-fund audit (1853), a farm-rent advertisement (1859), the Govanstown purchase (1866), a sons'-farm advertisement (1874), and agricultural-society activity (1878) -- confirming the family's continuous landholding and civic presence without adding new substantive facts to the chain of title.
Samuel Brady executed his will Nov 1 1862, later proved after his 1871 death, setting the terms for the estate succession that led to Sadtler trusteeship.
Brady died in December 1871; his 1862 will was proved Dec 15 1871, triggering estate succession leading to Sadtler trusteeship.
The 1877 Hopkins & Co. atlas plat georeferences the ballpark wedge, labeling it the Samuel Brady estate.
A portion of the historic Huntingdon tract was condemned for civic/road purposes in 1878, affecting Brady/Sadtler family holdings.
A period painting depicting the Brady family mansion on the estate was produced circa 1880.
A fire destroyed a shop operated by a Cross family member on or near the Brady estate lands.
Brady heirs leased a lot that became Oriole Park II (1889) and, later, Oriole Park IV, the immediate predecessor site.
An 1888 Baltimore City annexation is noted as bringing the Brady/Sadtler estate lands within city limits.
Samuel Brady Jr., a member of the family holding the estate, died in 1891, further complicating the multi-generational estate succession.
A boundary-line suit involving Brady heirs and the Chestnut Ridge tract was filed shortly before the Feb 1895 chancery decree.
The Feb 21 1895 chancery decree placed the Brady estate under court trusteeship, with Sadtler family members as trustees, setting up the 1899 sales.

Court-appointed trustees ran a series of 1899 sales of Brady estate parcels -- including a Wilcox alley sale (May 9), a four-parcel sale (May 29), and a sale of the 2900 Huntingdon parcel to Garrison establishing ground-rent ownership (May 31) -- preceding Hanlon's 1906 purchase.
A new ball club corporation, the Baltimore Baseball and Amusement Co., was organized, laying groundwork for the Union Park-era franchise that preceded Terrapin/Oriole Park V.
An injunction dispute arose over the Union Park baseball grounds, a predecessor venue in the same ownership orbit as the future Site V.
A newspaper report confirmed Sadtler family ownership of the York Road-area grounds destined to become the ballpark site.
Jack Dunn, the future Orioles owner and 1916 purchaser of Terrapin Park, arrived in Baltimore as a player, beginning his long association with the city's baseball scene.
A 1901 report noted boxing was barred at Union Park, naming both the Brady/Sadtler and the Garrison estate holdings as governing the restriction.
Mary Brady Sadtler, a key figure bridging the Brady and Sadtler family branches in the estate's trusteeship, died April 20 1902.
1905 conveyances -- Cook/Pentz transactions covering former Brady-Sadtler blocks (Sept 26 and Nov 16) -- further subdivided the estate's 25th Street-area tracts ahead of the Hanlon assembly.
The Union Park grounds -- a separate, earlier ballpark in the same ownership circle -- were sold in October 1905, a contextual marker distinct from the future Site V tract.
The entire remaining Brady tract sold to Harvey & Son for $200,000 on Nov 22 1906, five days before Hanlon's purchase of the ballpark parcel from Harvey & Son.
Hanlon purchased the Oriole Park parcel from Harvey & Son for roughly $50,000 on Nov 27 1906.
After his November 1906 purchase, Hanlon resold surrounding residential lots not needed for the ballpark, retaining the core parcel.
Hanlon sold a partial ownership interest in the ballpark grounds to a syndicate led by a Mr. White, briefly diluting his sole ownership.
By 1909 Hanlon had repurchased the White syndicate's interest and consolidated sole ownership, completing the Brady-Sadtler-Hanlon chain of title.
Jack Dunn purchased the Baltimore Orioles baseball club (the franchise, not yet the ground) from Ned Hanlon on Nov 16 1909.
A newspaper report assessed the residual value of former Sadtler estate lands adjoining the new ballpark grounds.
Hanlon engaged in negotiations with Boston baseball interests in 1911, part of his continuing involvement in professional baseball management alongside his Baltimore ground ownership.
A committee organized June 1 1911 to explore financing and construction options for a new Baltimore ballpark, an early precursor discussion to the 1914 Terrapin Park project.
Otto G. Simonson, who would design the 1914 ballpark, was arrested at the predecessor Oriole Park grounds in an incident unrelated to his later architectural role.
Simonson designed the 1914 ballpark to fit the wedge-shaped block, with his plan published Jan 27 1914.
Ned Hanlon toured the completed ballpark grounds days before the April 13 opening.

The new ballpark, initially named Terrapin Park for the Federal League Baltimore Terrapins, opened April 13 1914; a later retrospective in the Evening Sun ("When Baltimore Was Baseball Capital of the World") revisited the opening.
Jack Dunn sold Babe Ruth's contract to the Boston Red Sox in July 1914, a transaction connected to the Federal League's financial pressure on the Baltimore franchise.
The International League Orioles played their last 1914 home game at the new park amid mounting competitive pressure from the crosstown Federal League Terrapins.
The Federal League, whose Baltimore Terrapins played at the site, collapsed in 1915, precipitating the antitrust suit that would reach the U.S. Supreme Court in 1922.
A 1915 Sanborn fire-insurance map depicts both the Terrapin Park grounds and a nearby predecessor park as simultaneously operating structures.
The Baltimore Federal League club, based at the site, was named lead plaintiff in the antitrust suit against organized baseball, filed Jan 6 1915.
A boxing card featuring a Williams-Taylor bout was staged at the predecessor Terrapin Park name for the grounds, prior to Dunn's 1916 purchase and renaming.
Federal League president James Gilmore sent a telegram addressing the league's collapsing finances in December 1915, shortly before its dissolution and Dunn's purchase of the park.
Hanlon, having sold the ballpark ground, joined the city's Park Board around 1916-1917, later heading it by 1931.
Jack Dunn purchased the ballpark grounds for $25,000 in March 1916, following the Federal League's collapse, and renamed the site Oriole Park.
Jack Dunn incorporated 29th Street Realty Co. on Mar 6 1916 as the corporate vehicle to hold title to the ballpark grounds.
The first documented boxing card under Jack Dunn's new ownership was staged at the ballpark July 8 1916.
A boxing match between Levinsky and Dillon was held at the site July 13 1916.
Bantamweight champion Kid Williams fought Frankie Brown at the site Sept 4 1916.
An AAA-sanctioned open-air boxing card featuring Loadman and Root was held at the site June 22 1917.
The Baltimore club (the "Baltfeds") formally filed its antitrust suit against organized baseball in September 1917.
Kid Williams fought Young Chaney in a card benefiting war-savings-stamp sales, June 1 1918.
A proposed Jack Dempsey vs. Fred Fulton bout at the site, floated June 24 1918, did not come to pass.
A Red Cross benefit boxing card on June 29 1918 saw Johnny Dundee fail to appear against Chaney; a follow-up July 16 1918 letter corroborates that police subsequently banned boxing at the site.
A newspaper advertisement promoted a Boston Red Sox barnstorming exhibition at the site, Sept 19 1918.
The International League Orioles, playing at Oriole Park, began a run of seven consecutive pennants from 1919 through 1925.
Ned Hanlon gave trial testimony April 1 1919 in the Federal Baseball Club antitrust case.
Babe Ruth, by then with the Red Sox, hit four home runs in an exhibition game at his former home ballpark.
The day after his four-homer game, Ruth both pitched and hit two additional home runs in a follow-up exhibition at the site.
Boxing cards resumed at the ballpark June 13 1919 after the wartime police ban was lifted.
A boxing card featuring Black fighters as the headline attraction was staged at the site in June 1919, including a Leo Johnson vs. Young Joe Gans bout.
A July 4 1919 holiday boxing card was staged at the site.
A multi-event athletic carnival was staged at the ballpark, July 15 1919.
The Philadelphia Phillies played the Dry Docks amateur/service team in an exhibition game at the site, July 20 1919.
A Mason-Daly boxing match was held at the site in late July 1919.
A less-certain report credits Ruth with two additional home runs in a September 1919 exhibition against the Dry Docks team at the site.
The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia reversed the trial court's verdict in the Federal Baseball Club case in 1920.
Future Hall of Famer Lefty Grove pitched for the International League Orioles at the site from 1920 to 1924, prior to his sale to the Philadelphia Athletics.
A 1920 boxing card featured Williams against Brandt, paired with a Ray-Smith bout, at the site.
A riot broke out among fans at the ballpark Aug 10 1920, resulting in arrests of named individuals reported by the press.
A boxing match featuring a fighter named Ertle was held at the site Aug 13 1920.
A Ruth exhibition appearance at the site on Apr 8 1921 drew a reported crowd of 8,000.
A scholastic baseball series between Baltimore City College and Polytechnic Institute was played at the site, Apr 16 1921.
The ballpark hosted an inaugural "schoolboy day" welcoming students as spectator guests, June 20 1921, later documented in a period photograph.

A June 20 1921 boxing rematch between Tiplitz and Rice ended in a crowd riot amid allegations the fight had been fixed; Jack Dunn was quoted expressing displeasure, and concessionaire "Cousin Romey" was noted working the event.
A tournament featuring military boxers was staged at the ballpark, July 2 1921.
Police were called to the ballpark to quell a disturbance during a game against the Toronto club, Aug 12 1921.
A dispute over rental terms between the boxing promoter and 29th Street Realty temporarily halted boxing cards at the venue in 1922, preceding the move to Westport.
The Supreme Court ruled May 29 1922 that baseball was exempt from antitrust law, a landmark decision originating from the Baltimore Federal League club based at this site.
Regular boxing promotion relocated from Oriole Park to a Westport venue, July 24 1922, amid a rental dispute that had already begun disrupting cards earlier that year.
A less-certain account credits Ruth with three home runs in a Sept 1922 exhibition against an Army team at the site.
A retrospective feature by sportswriter Lantz reviewed the ballpark's first decade, published Mar 23 1924.
Connie Mack's Philadelphia Athletics played an exhibition game at the site on Apr 6 1924.
The schoolboy-day tradition continued as an annual event at the ballpark, documented June 15 1925.
A feature story profiled Orioles pitching star Jack Ogden, published Aug 20 1927 during the team's pennant-era run.
A 1928 photograph documents local social "pleasure clubs" gathered at or near the ballpark.
Jack Dunn, owner of the Orioles and the ballpark ground since 1916, died Oct 22 1928, leaving the estate to be managed in trust.
A separate 1929 proposal floated developing the ballpark grounds into a broader municipal sports center.
A syndicate led by promoter Ferrer, with boxing figure Leo Flynn, proposed converting or supplementing the site with a multi-sport arena; the plan was never realized.
Bill Gibson wrote that Oriole Park again shut its gates to Black players, forcing the Black Sox to Maryland Park.
A May 1 1930 exhibition is cited, less certainly, as Ruth's final appearance at his former home ballpark.
The Knot Hole Gang program launched July 29 1930, giving boys free or discounted admission to Orioles games at the site.
A 1931 photograph captures Babe Ruth at bat during one of his exhibition-era return visits to the site.
An intercity police-department baseball game against Camden, N.J. officers was played at the site, July 16 1931.
A box-lacrosse exhibition event was staged at the venue in 1932.
A charity baseball game pitting police officers against City Hall staff was played at the site, Aug 24 1932.
The Baltimore Afro-American launched its Jim Crow boycott campaign against the ballpark's segregated "first base pavilion" policy beginning Apr 22 1933, with a follow-up editorial Apr 29 1933.
Orioles general manager Dawson was quoted May 6 1933 defending the ballpark's segregated seating policy amid the ongoing boycott campaign.
The Kiwanis Club sponsored a "donkey baseball" novelty charity event at the site in September 1934.
Maryland's boxing commission levied a fine against a fighter named Rivers for conduct at a 1935 card held at the site.
The Century Athletic Club began a regular Friday-night boxing series at the site starting June 3 1935, debuting formally June 7.
Boxer Eddie Ross headlined a Century Athletic Club card at the site, June 28 1935.
An intercity police-department baseball game against Alexandria, Va. officers was played at the site, July 7 1935.
A Federal Bureau of Investigation baseball team played a game at the site, July 13 1935.
The Monarch Athletic Club staged a boxing card at the site, July 15 1936.
A 1937 aerial photograph documents the ballpark's footprint and the surrounding Waverly neighborhood.
29th Street Realty arranged in April 1937 to open the ballpark to Negro National League Sunday games, ending years of exclusion and paving the way for the Elite Giants' tenancy.
The federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation's georeferenced 1937 Residential Security Map graded the ballpark's blocks "C4," with adjacent "D"-graded areas 30-35% Black.
The Baltimore Elite Giants made their Negro National League home debut at the ballpark May 16 1937, facing the Pittsburgh Crawfords with catcher Biz Mackey behind the plate.
A doubleheader between the Hilldale Club and the Bacharach Giants was played at the ballpark, Aug 15 1937.
A Sept 14 1937 report references an Elite Giants night-game matchup connected to a Glen Burnie-area opponent.
A Negro National League championship playoff game between the Homestead Grays and Chicago American Giants was hosted at the site, Sept 26 1937.
The Elite Giants split part of their 1938 schedule between Oriole Park and Bugle Field, prior to fully returning to Oriole Park as their primary home in 1939.
The Tall Cedars fraternal organization held a themed night event at the site in June 1938.
An interracial all-star exhibition organized by George Scales featured major leaguer Jimmie Foxx facing Negro League talent at the site, Oct 9 1938.
The Elite Giants formally announced Oriole Park as their primary home grounds for the 1939 season, Jan 7 1939.
The Elite Giants' 1939 home opener, May 14 1939, featured Hall of Famers Josh Gibson and Buck Leonard among the visiting Homestead Grays.
A June 18 1939 doubleheader at the site featured future Hall of Famer Monte Irvin and slugger Mule Suttles.
A lopsided game on July 9 1939, in which the teams combined for roughly 30 hits, ended in a forfeit at the site.
A July 22 1939 photograph documents an Elite Giants game against a Cuban League touring club at the site.
An Aug 10 1939 photograph documents an amateur trade-league baseball tournament held at the site.
A published box score documents an Elite Giants doubleheader against the New York Cubans, Aug 27 1939.
A civic figure named McMowbray, active in Waverly-area real-estate finance, was the subject of a financial-practices inquiry reported Aug 31 1939.

The Elite Giants won the 1939 Negro National League championship in a series against the Homestead Grays played at Oriole Park, including a Sept 17 game 2 in which Josh Gibson homered and a game 3 that ended in a curfew-shortened tie.
The Elite Giants swept a series against the Newark Eagles to clinch their berth in the 1939 NNL championship series, culminating Sept 16 1939.
A Waverly-area housing study published Oct 4 1939 introduced greenlining-style framing intended to counter the 1937 HOLC redlining designation.
An interracial all-star baseball exhibition was held at the ballpark, Oct 8 1939.
A 1940 reference cites the ballpark's seating capacity as 14,000, down from the 16,000 capacity at its 1914 opening.
An advertisement promoted McMowbray's FHA-backed home-lending services in the Waverly area, Mar 31 1940.
A promotional booklet touting the Waverly neighborhood's amenities, including the ballpark, was distributed starting May 12 1940.
Roy Campanella hit two home runs as the Elite Giants swept a doubleheader at the site, July 18 1940, before a crowd of roughly 4,000.
A doubleheader involving four different Negro League clubs was staged at the site, Aug 18 1940.
A second interracial all-star doubleheader bill was staged at the site, Oct 13 1940, continuing the prior year's interracial exhibition series.
The contract for the Chalky Wright vs. Jackie Wilson "colored" featherweight championship bout was signed July 10 1941, a week before the fight.

Chalky Wright defeated Jackie Wilson for the "colored" featherweight title at the site, July 17 1941, with the boxing ring erected between the pitcher's mound and home plate; the bout, moved from Municipal Stadium, drew a reported 10,000-seat gate.
The Elite Giants completed a 13-game home winning streak at the site, reported July 26 1941.
An Aug 9 1941 game at the site featured three future Hall of Famers -- Leon Day, Monte Irvin, and Roy Campanella -- on the field simultaneously.
The Newark Eagles defeated the Elite Giants in a wild, high-scoring game at the site Aug 16 1941, documented in both box-score coverage and a period photograph of the Eagles at first base.
The Elite Giants swept a series against the New York Black Yankees at the site, concluding Sept 6 1941.

The Elite Giants' last opening day at the site, May 10 1942, drew roughly 5,500 fans; Roy Campanella delivered a bases-loaded single for the winning hit, but rowdy-fan complaints from neighbors intensified in the game's wake.
A help-wanted advertisement sought concession-stand workers for the ballpark, published May 16 1942.
Neighborhood objections to Black fans' noise led to the Elite Giants' permanent relocation to Bugle Field by May 30 1942.
The International League Orioles played a doubleheader against the Montreal Royals at the site, June 5 1942.
Chalky Wright defended his featherweight title against Harry Jeffra at the site, winning by TKO in round 10 before a crowd of roughly 6,000 and a purse of $7,500.
Chalky Wright, twice a title-fight winner/defender at the site in 1941-42, appeared on the cover of Ring magazine in December 1942.
Mary Dunn, widow of Jack Dunn and trustee of the estate holding the ballpark ground, died in February 1943.
The International League Orioles released their 1943 season schedule for the site, published Feb 4 1943 amid wartime travel restrictions.
A profile of heavyweight Harry Bobo, who would fight at the site later that year, noted he had been denied an army boxing license, published Mar 13 1943.
An amateur baseball day at the site, June 27 1943, featured an appearance by Mayor Theodore McKeldin.
A heavyweight bout between Harry Bobo and Murray was billed as Baltimore's biggest fight show, with 15,000 seats available at the site, Aug 9 1943.
A youth baseball instructional school associated with the nickname "Bird" was held at the site, Aug 12 1943.
A youth "midget league" championship game, won by a St. Bernardine's parish team, was played at the ballpark, Aug 30 1943.
Despite losing their home ballpark mid-season, the Orioles won the 1944 International League championship and the Junior World Series, playing out of Municipal Stadium.
The New York Giants played an exhibition game against the International League Orioles at the site, Apr 1 1944.
A letter from a resident named Blocher, published Apr 21 1944, escalated decades of neighborhood complaints about noise and late-running games/events at the ballpark.
A fan named Norman Bell filed suit seeking $250 in damages after being injured by a foul ball at the ballpark, reported June 9 1944.
A June 16 1944 report noted that wartime material shortages had precluded scheduling football at the ballpark that year.
A Sheppard-Murray boxing rematch, held June 19 1944, was the last documented event at the site, 15 days before the fire, with a gate above $30,000.
The final baseball game played at the ballpark, July 3 1944 against Syracuse, featured a grand slam by a player named Carson, the day before the fire.

An eight-alarm fire destroyed the ballpark's wooden grandstand on July 4 1944, causing an estimated $150,000 loss including Jack Dunn's trophies, ending 30 seasons of baseball at the site; every seat for an upcoming event had reportedly already been sold, and neighborhood property damage was estimated at $22,000-$50,000.
Fire investigators reported July 5 1944 that a carelessly discarded cigarette was the likely cause of the previous day's blaze.
An Associated Press dispatch, July 5 1944, reported the Orioles' games would be postponed and then relocated following the fire.
The displaced Orioles played their first home game at Municipal Stadium on July 16 1944, having relocated after the fire.
A soldier's published letter criticized Mayor McKeldin's handling of the ballpark site's aftermath, accompanied by a photograph, July 24 1944.
A human-interest feature published Aug 4 1944 described the Waverly neighborhood as feeling "lonesome" in the weeks after the fire ended ballpark activity.
An Aug 12 1944 retrospective piece characterized the destroyed ballpark as a cozy "bandbox" venue.
Record crowds at the Orioles' temporary Municipal Stadium home, reported Aug 30 1944, spurred early planning discussions for a permanent replacement stadium.
Jackie Robinson played at Municipal Stadium with the Montreal Royals in 1946, confirming that Baltimore's organized-baseball games had permanently moved off the destroyed Oriole Park site.
A March 20 1948 article looked back on years of neighbor nuisance litigation connected to the former ballpark, in the context of the site's postwar redevelopment discussions.
A Salvation Army building was constructed circa 1950 on a portion of the former ballpark site, part of its postwar redevelopment.
The Diamond Cab Company introduced a city rezoning bill, May 27 1952, seeking to redevelop part of the former ballpark site for a cab facility.
McMowbray, the Waverly-area lending figure, was reported serving on a local real-estate board, Nov 30 1952.
A revised version of the Diamond Cab rezoning ordinance was introduced Mar 24 1953.
A city councilman named Hubbard publicly supported the Diamond Cab rezoning bill, Apr 16 1953.
A broader neighborhood redevelopment plan for Waverly, encompassing the former ballpark site, was unveiled May 28 1953.
The Diamond Cab Company withdrew its rezoning bid for the former ballpark land, Oct 14 1953, leaving the site's redevelopment path open.
The St. Louis Browns relocated to Baltimore in 1954 and adopted the Orioles name, a franchise-history footnote connecting the modern MLB Orioles to the club that once played at this site.
A contract bringing an RC Cola bottling plant to the former ballpark site was confirmed in November 1954.
An Evening Sun report of Nov 19 1954 named the then-current owner of the vacant former ballpark parcel amid ongoing redevelopment interest.
A newspaper advertisement, Dec 27 1956, documented construction progress on the new RC Cola bottling plant, including a call for electricians.
RC Cola completed its relocation of bottling operations to the newly constructed plant on the former ballpark site in 1957.
RC Cola ran an advertisement tied to National Brotherhood Week, Feb 14 1959, at its plant on the former ballpark site.
RC Cola general manager Burchem stated in a 1962 advertisement that 35% of the plant's 125 employees at the former ballpark site were Black.
A local real-estate board report used "blight" language to describe conditions in the district surrounding the former ballpark, Apr 26 1964.
RC Cola placed a help-wanted advertisement for a route salesman at its plant on the former ballpark site, June 29 1969, confirming continued operations there.
Beverage Capital Corp. was confirmed as the operator/owner of the former RC Cola bottling plant on the site, Aug 3 1987.
29th Street Realty Co., the Dunn family's 1916 corporate vehicle for the ballpark ground, was formally dissolved in 1988, decades after the underlying property had passed through other hands.
Baltimore sportswriter John Steadman publicly campaigned in 1995 for Ned Hanlon's induction into the National Baseball Hall of Fame.
Baltimore Sun columnist Jacques Kelly published a July 4 1995 retrospective on the ballpark's history, naming period neighborhood figures and businesses connected to the site.
Ned Hanlon, the ballpark ground's early owner and longtime Baltimore baseball figure, was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1996.
Beverage Capital Corp. sold the former ballpark/bottling-plant parcel to Bevco Realty in 2010, a milestone ownership transfer consolidated from the era's routine financing filings.
Bevco Realty sold the parcel to 2900 Loch Raven LLC in 2011, another milestone transfer in the modern ownership chain preceding the brewery's arrival.
Peabody Heights Brewery was founded in 2012 and began converting the former bottling-plant building on the site into a working brewery.
A War of 1812 bicentennial walking-tour program, launched Apr 1 2012, included the site in recognition of Colonel Biays's Battle of North Point role.
The Waverly Main Street Historic District, encompassing the former ballpark site, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, effective Dec 31 2013.
The Old Oriole Park site/brewery redevelopment received a local Bohemian-sponsored preservation or business award in 2015.
401 E. 30th Street LLC, the entity behind Peabody Heights Brewery, formally acquired title to the brewery parcel of the site in 2015, consolidating ownership under the brewery's operating entity.

A roughly $500,000 Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development economic-development loan helped finance Peabody Heights Brewery's launch on the site, distinct from the routine bank refinancing instruments recorded in the same period.
A 2015 survey by the S. J. Martenet Company, conducted by surveyor Anne Leininger, located home plate, the pitcher's mound, and the bases within the modern parcel boundaries.
The Salvation Army acquired the separately titled south parcel of the former ballpark site on Sept 16 2015.
A dispute arose between the Maryland Historical Society and Peabody Heights Brewery over usage rights to historic ballpark photographs, reported Apr 8 2016.
Cane Collective, a food/beverage business entity later associated with the site, was organized Sept 1 2017.
DMG Foods opened as a tenant business at the Peabody Heights Brewery site, Mar 7 2018.
Major League Baseball formally recognized seven Negro Leagues, including the Negro National League in which the Elite Giants played at this site, as major leagues, Dec 16 2020.
DMG Foods closed its operation at the Peabody Heights Brewery site in February 2021.
BARCO Commissary, a shared commercial-kitchen operation, opened at the site in 2022, succeeding DMG Foods as a tenant use.
Cane Collective formally registered its business tradename with the state, July 24 2023.
Major League Baseball integrated Negro Leagues player statistics, including those of Elite Giants players who competed at this site, into its official historical record book, May 29 2024.
A 2025 documentation of BARCO Commissary lists its current roster of food-business tenants operating at the site.
Cane Collective announced new pickup/retail operations at the site, Jan 31 2025.
Cane Collective underwent a corporate restructuring, effective Mar 21 2025.

As of 2026, the historic Old Oriole Park (V) footprint remains split between two separately titled parcels: the brewery parcel held by 401 E. 30th Street LLC and the south parcel held by the Salvation Army.

Samuel H. Taggert, acting as court-appointed trustee, deeded a tract on the east side of the York Turnpike to George C. H. Coffield. This deed, recorded in Baltimore County Liber JHL No. 43, folio 548, is the earliest documented root of title for the 3117 Greenmount parcel; later deeds describe the lot relative to the northwest corner of the Coffield tract.

The Coffield deed was executed only eight to nine weeks after Maryland's third constitution abolished slavery effective November 1, 1864. The white paper flags, but does not resolve, whether grantee George C. H. Coffield was African American, which would make this an early act of Black property ownership on the corridor.

A sheriff's notice recorded a mechanic's-lien writ of scire facias brought by Samuel Burns (surviving partner of Burns & Sloan) against property owner George C. H. Coffield and builder William Funk, seeking $334.41 for work and materials dating from January 1, 1865, on a two-story frame dwelling/store fronting about 59 feet on the York Turnpike.
Henry C. Zoll, later the operator of a livery stable near the 3117 site, married Emma Stewart in Baltimore on May 15, 1873.

Newspaper notices from 1873 and 1874 identify Charles S. Hamilton as proprietor of the newly opened Waverly Hotel on York Road, part of the York Road village node later redeveloped as the Greenmount Avenue commercial corridor.

The 1877 Hopkins 'Plan of Waverly, 9th Dist.' (Atlas of Baltimore County, Maryland) cadastrally places 'Chas. S. Hamilton' at the York Road/Waverly Avenue intersection, the same pre-Greenmount node later associated with the Zoll livery and the 3117-3119 Greenmount site.
A newspaper personnel listing names Henry Zoll among the conductors of the Baltimore-Towsontown line of the York Road Railway.
A Baltimore Sun item describes Henry C. Zoll as 'a farmer on the York road, near Govanstown,' who brought a thirty-inch, twelve-pound red beet to the Sun's office.

Henry Zoll left his York Road Railway conductor job to enter the livery and express business at Waverly in partnership with Mr. Dentry, forming Dentry & Zoll, which erected a large stable next to the Waverly Hotel.

A newspaper eyewitness account of a meteor sighting places Henry Zoll standing near the Waverly Police Station, confirming his continued residence/business presence in the Waverly village core as of mid-1888.

The 1893 Polk's Directory lists a 'Hamilton Chas.' at 908 York Road. The white paper explicitly cautions that this listing documents Hamilton's broader York Road presence but should be treated as a separate, non-conflated property from the Waverly Hotel/3117 node.

An 1899 advertisement by James S. Bateman documents a business stand fronting on both York Road and Old York Road at the 1023/101 address pairing, demonstrating that parcels in this section of the corridor could front both streets.
The 1903 Polk's Baltimore City Directory lists Henry C. Zoll's livery business at 1027 York Road, within the address bracket later associated with the Coffield root of title.
A Baltimore Sun classified advertised a sorrel horse for sale at 'Henry C. Zoll's Stable, 1027 York road,' confirming the stable's continued operation at that address.

A court-ordered trustee's sale (Crain & Hershey, solicitors; Omer F. Hershey, Trustee) sold the 'Desirable Stable Property, 1027 York Road' on March 14, 1904, reciting verbatim the metes-and-bounds tracing to the 1865 Coffield deed and describing the parcel as improved by a two-story frame stable, subject to an annual ground rent of $175.

A Baltimore Sun classified advertised a combination riding and driving horse at 'Zoll's Waverly Stables, 1027 York road, opp. Waverly ave.,' confirming the stable's continued operation up to the eve of the Greenmount Avenue renumbering.

Baltimore City Ordinance 09-269 took effect March 10, 1909, amending the general plan of streets for territory annexed in 1888 and formalizing the transition of the corridor's naming from York Road/York Turnpike Road toward Greenmount Avenue.

A 1914 Baltimore Sun listing identifies Hamilton Stampaugh at 3119 Greenmount Avenue in connection with a Maxwell automobile, showing that the modern numbered Greenmount address sequence had reached the site by 1914.

Polk's Baltimore City directories for 1915 and 1917 list a livery (stable) operated by W. C. & Son (William C. and Reynolds Childs) at 3117 Greenmount Avenue; proprietor William C. Childs resided nearby at 3110 Greenmount. This establishes that the parcel carried a frame livery stable, not the present brick showroom, well into the late 1910s.
A Firestone dealer advertisement lists United Garage Co., Inc. at 345 E. 33rd Street, three years before the firm relocated to the 3117-3119 Greenmount site.

A Baltimore Sun dealer listing identifies United Garage Co., Inc. at 3119 Greenmount Avenue, placing an automobile-service business on the 3117-3119 site roughly eighteen months before the Miller Brothers redevelopment.
A Baltimore City building-code notice records that J. H. Deitrich applied on September 18, 1926 to use the front and rear of 3117 Greenmount Avenue for signs, under the city's Building Code.

The Baltimore Sun reported that Miller Brothers Furniture Company, Inc. leased the lot for 99 years from Mrs. Lula S. Dietrich at $1,200/year (on a $20,000 valuation) through brokers Lee E. Hartman & Co. The old 35-by-140-foot frame warehouse was to be replaced by a two-story-and-basement brick and concrete showroom and warehouse of about 10,500 square feet, with the construction contract awarded to E. Eyring & Sons Co. at a cost of about $30,000 and completion expected in about three months.
A follow-up Baltimore Sun notice confirms the 99-year lease of the 3117 Greenmount lot through Lee E. Hartman & Co. by Miller Brothers Furniture Company, Inc.

Erhard Eyring's son John F. Eyring is documented as 'a fine theater architect' responsible for buildings including the Catholic Center, the Arcade and Pikes theaters, St. Francis of Assisi Catholic Church, and the Liberty Savings & Loan building. The white paper identifies him only as a plausible, unconfirmed candidate for having designed the 3117 showroom built by his family's construction firm.
Erhard Eyring founded the construction firm E. Eyring & Sons Co. in Highlandtown in 1887; the firm would later build the 3117 Greenmount showroom in 1928 and go on to acquire it as owner in 1933.

Maryland SDAT's Real Property Data Search record for 3117 Greenmount lists a primary-structure-built date of 1920. The white paper treats this administrative date as most likely a stale entry carried forward from the prior frame warehouse/livery, in conflict with the firmer March 1928 newspaper evidence of new brick-and-concrete construction.

A full-page Congoleum Gold Seal Rugs 'Six-Day Special Sale' dealer advertisement names Miller Bros. Furniture Co. at 3117 Greenmount Ave., the earliest in-hand evidence of the firm operating from the newly built showroom.

A full-page Sparton Radio advertisement lists Miller Bros. Furniture Co., Inc., 3117 Greenmount Ave. (phone Homewood 9188) as a dealer, and Miller Brothers advertised the Sparton Equasonne Model 930 radio at $189.50 that year.
A merchant-association advertisement titled 'First, Furnish Your Home' lists Miller Bros. Furniture Co., 3117 Greenmount Ave. among selected Baltimore furniture merchants.
A 1930 Better Bedding Week advertisement lists Miller Bros. Furniture Co., Inc., 3117 Greenmount Avenue as a dealer for Conscience Brand mattresses and box springs.
A 1931 advertisement lists Miller Bros. as a dealer for the Easy 2-Tub Damp-Dryer Washer, documenting the firm's expansion into home appliances shortly before its 1932 bankruptcy.
The Baltimore Sun ran a 'Bankrupt Sale!' advertisement for Miller Bros. Furniture Co., Inc., 3117-19 Greenmount Ave., announcing the firm had only five days left and must vacate the premises.
The Evening Sun reported that Klecka, Levy & Russy of 2232-34 East Monument Street had bought out the entire remaining bankrupt stock of Miller Bros. Furniture Co., Inc.
E. T. Newell & Co. advertised a trustees' sale of the property at '3117 Greenmount Avenue, Near 33rd Street,' scheduled for Monday, November 21, 1932, at 2 P.M.

At the November 21, 1932 trustees' auction, B. Franklin Zipp, acting as agent, purchased the property for a bid of $19,000. The lot was described as approximately 35 by 126 feet, running back to Old York Road. The sale was conducted for trustees James L. Hennegan and George L. Lochboehler through E. T. Newell & Co.

A December 1932 business-property classified advertisement, placed through brokers C. A. & C. M. Diffenderffer, described 3117 Greenmount as a '2-story-and-basement modern brick building, 35 x 100, elevator, large show windows... just below 33rd St., finest shopping district.'

Trustees James L. Hennegan and George L. Lochboehler deeded 3117 Greenmount Avenue to Eyring Realty Corporation — the same firm that had built the showroom as contractor in 1928 — for a consideration of about $19,000 in fee, reported publicly two weeks later.

The Baltimore Sun reported that Eyring Realty Corporation leased the 3117 Greenmount building to Century Furniture Company through brokers C. A. and C. M. Diffenderffer, citing approximately 10,500 square feet of floor space and including an option to purchase.
A May 31, 1933 notice names B. H. Buckholz as associated with Century Furniture Co., 3117-3119 Greenmount Ave.
A help-wanted advertisement for three salesmen for 'our newly opened elec. appliance dept.' documents Century Furniture Co.'s expansion into electric appliances at 3117 Greenmount.
Frigidaire dealer-list advertisements in 1934 and 1935 name Century Furniture Company, 3117 Greenmount Ave., as an authorized dealer.
Help-wanted advertisements state 'THE CENTURY FURNITURE CO. has openings... See MR. DALE,' naming a manager-level contact for the firm.

A July 5, 1934 door-to-door sales recruitment advertisement placed by Century Furniture Co. explicitly specifies 'white' applicants, documenting the racially discriminatory hiring norms common to Baltimore retail employment advertising of the era.

An Evening Sun display advertisement promoted '3 Rooms' of furniture for $248 and listed Hecht's Furniture House locations at 930-32-34-36-38 S. Charles Street and 3117-3119 Greenmount Ave., marking Hecht's takeover of the building from Century Furniture.

General Electric dealer lists in the Evening Sun and Baltimore Sun continued to name Hecht's Furniture House at 3117 Greenmount Ave. through at least August 1936, with Omar Hipsley identified as the contact/manager at that location.

T. C. W. Hobbs Co., Inc. held a public auction sale of 'an excellent stock of new furniture' within the warehouse at 3117 Greenmount Avenue, beginning June 25, 1936 and continuing nightly through at least June 29, 1936, conducted jointly with auctioneers E. T. Newell & Co.

A Cumberland Evening Times chain advertisement lists '3117-19 Greenmount Ave., Baltimore, Md.' first among the Joe the Motorists' Friend chain's stores, under 'Cut Rate Auto Accessories, Tires, Sporting Goods and Radio Supplies,' marking the building's turnover from furniture retail to the regional auto-and-sporting-goods chain.
A 1937 city directory cited in the National Register registration form shows the building occupied by Joe the Motorist's auto accessories store.

A 1940 Cumberland Evening Times Red Tag Sale advertisement documents the chain's broad merchandise range: auto radios, seat covers, motor oil, tires, batteries, fishing tackle, bicycles, lawn and garden goods, cameras, paint, toys, and sporting goods.
A 1949 Baltimore Sun recruitment advertisement sought future store managers at Joe the Motorist's Friend, Inc., 3117-19 Greenmount Ave.
An Evening Sun advertisement titled 'Smash Values' listed 3117-19 Greenmount Ave. alongside a second chain location at 415-19 S. Conkling St.
An August 1950 recruitment advertisement named Marvin Shney in connection with the Joe the Motorists' Friend store at 3117-19 Greenmount Avenue.
By 1954, chain advertising described Joe the Motorists' Friend as having grown to '20 Great Stores,' still listing the 3117-19 Greenmount Avenue location.
By late 1955, Cumberland advertising described the Joe the Motorists' Friend chain as encompassing '22 Great Stores,' shortly before the chain's departure from 3117 Greenmount by 1957.

A Baltimore Sun advertisement for 'Kiddie Land' at 3117 Greenmount Avenue advertised a Siebert tricycle, marking the earliest documented appearance of Paul Engelman's toy and hobby business at the site.

Peter G. Engelman graduated from Baltimore City College High School in 1957 and initially worked in his father Paul Engelman's toy and hobby store at 3117 Greenmount before leaving for a career in accounting.

An advertisement for Engelman's Kiddie Land, 3117 Greenmount Ave., advertising a tricycle, explicitly claimed the store offered 'Over 10,000 sq. ft. of toys' — a figure that closely echoes the 10,500-square-foot showroom cited in the 1928 construction notice and the 1933 Century Furniture lease.
A Waverly Shopping District merchants' co-op advertisement in the Evening Sun lists Engelman's Kiddie Land, 3117 Greenmount Ave., among approximately 30 named 'Park Free' merchants.
A classified advertisement offered Varney HO model trains, brand new for $20 discounted to $7.95 cash, from Engelman's Kiddie Land, 3117 Greenmount Ave.
A display advertisement under the 'Engelman's Kiddie-Land' masthead offered toys at discount prices, including a Mattel Winchester Rifle, Remco Bull Dog Tank, Tiny Tears Doll, and tricycles.

A display advertisement identifies 'Engelman's, 3117 Greenmount Ave.' as a coin dealer buying and selling old coins with free appraisals, containing no reference to toys, signaling that the Kiddieland retail program had wound down by early 1961.

A classified advertisement documented the terminal liquidation of Engelman's remaining stock: 'Swimming Pools — Selling out. Below cost. Engelman's. 3117 Greenmount,' marking the definitive end of the Kiddieland business at the address.
A Baltimore Sun engagement notice announced Miss Ellen L. Shofer's engagement to Pvt. Peter G. Engelman, USA, son of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Engelman of 3216 Hatton Road.

A Baltimore Sun item names Paul Engelman as in charge of the investment department of Nathanson Real Estate, with more than $200,000 available for property purchases, his first documented post-retail career move after the Kiddieland business closed.
A Mal Sherman Realtor display advertisement in the Baltimore Afro-American lists two properties under licensed agent Paul Engelman.

An advertisement for a real estate licensing preparation course names 'Paul Engelman Realtor,' showing that by 1972 he was operating independently under his own name rather than through another brokerage.

Paul Engelman, the Czech-Jewish refugee lawyer turned Baltimore toy retailer and later realtor who ran Engelman's Kiddieland at 3117 Greenmount, died on December 4, 1976 at his home on Hatton Road, Baltimore, survived by his wife Doris and sons Peter and Jerry.

A Baltimore Sun display advertisement documents Moses Zalis conducting a 'Removal Sale' at 819 Greenmount Ave., the pre-renumbering address for 3117, advertising living room, bedroom, and dining room suites at reduced prices with free delivery.

A Greenmount Avenue corridor address renumbering, bracketed to May 22-23, 1971, converted the address 819 Greenmount Avenue (used in Moses Zalis's February 1971 ad) to the modern 3117 Greenmount Avenue.
A 1972 Baltimore Sun classified advertisement lists Moses Zallis, 3117 Greenmount Ave., offering a bedroom suite.
A September 1987 advertisement lists Moses Zalis, 3117 Greenmount Ave., advertising bunk beds with free city delivery and setup.

A December 1989 Evening Sun display advertisement identifies Moses Zalis Furniture, 3117 Greenmount Ave., advertising bunk beds with bedding and free city delivery, the last documented appearance of the Zalis furniture tenancy.

Dorothy Dietrich, Wilhelmina Dietrich, and Helen Dietrich Butler, heirs of the Dietrich family that had ground-leased the lot to Miller Brothers in 1928, deeded fee title in the property to Eyring, converting Eyring from ground lessee/building owner into fee owner as well.
An internal deed dated May 3, 1948 transferred the property from Eyring Realty Corporation to an affiliated entity, Eyring Realty Enterprises, Inc.

Edward Eyring, son of founder Erhard Eyring, headed E. Eyring & Sons Co. from 1932 to 1964, the same period in which the firm's affiliated Eyring Realty Corporation acquired and owned 3117 Greenmount.
Edward Erhard Eyring Sr., grandson of founder Erhard Eyring, joined E. Eyring & Sons Co. in 1941, eventually operating the firm until closing it in 1977.
Edward Erhard Eyring Sr. retired and closed E. Eyring & Sons Co. in 1977, ending 90 years of operation by the firm that built the 3117 Greenmount showroom in 1928.
Edward Erhard Eyring Sr., retired president of E. Eyring & Sons Co. and the third-generation family member connected to the firm that built 3117 Greenmount, died March 19, 2009 at age 89.

Florence Crittenton Mission Incorporated conveyed 3113, 3115, and 3117 Greenmount Avenue together with 3100 and 3102 Old York Road to Eyring Realty Enterprises, Inc. for $2,500, executed July 18, 1988 and recorded August 26, 1988.

The same 1988 conveyance deed explicitly states that the leasehold estate described in the December 30, 1936 Dietrich deed 'shall merge with that portion of the reversion herein, and the annual ground rent as to 3117 Greenmount Avenue shall be forever extinguished,' ending the 60-year-old annual ground rent obligation originating in the 1928 Miller Brothers lease.

Forty-two days after acquiring the consolidated parcels, Eyring Realty Enterprises, Inc. conveyed 3117 Greenmount Avenue to Jin Pyo Hong and Auk J. Hong for $115,000; the same day, the Hongs executed a purchase-money deed of trust for $86,250 to Banking Services Corp.
Jin Pyo Hong and Auk J. Hong conveyed 3117 Greenmount Avenue to Nam Seo Koo and Seon Gyu Koo for $175,000, executed December 24, 1992 and recorded January 7, 1993.

Simultaneous with their purchase, the Koos executed a Deed of Trust and Security Agreement with NationsBank of Maryland, N.A. securing a $131,000 commercial loan, listing their notice address as 'c/o New York Fashions, Inc., 210 West Lexington Street, Baltimore,' directly tying the Koo ownership to the New York Fashions apparel chain that would occupy the building as 'New Issue.'

Following the departure of Moses Zalis Furniture (last documented December 1989), the building's commercial program shifted to apparel retail under the Koo ownership period. Web-based business-directory research identifies the tenant as New York Fashions, a multi-location Baltimore women's and juniors clothing chain, operating at 3117 Greenmount under the store name 'New Issue' (phone [phone redacted], contact Sonja Rabuli).

Bank of America, N.A. (successor to NationsBank of Maryland, N.A.) appointed PRLAP, Inc. as substitute trustee and issued a Certificate of Satisfaction confirming the Koos' 1992 deed of trust was fully paid and discharged after a fourteen-year financing term.

A Baltimore Sun Watchdog article by Liz Kay, reporting on the temporary closure of the adjacent Waverly Firehouse (Engine 31, 3123 Greenmount Avenue), includes a Gene Sweeney Jr. photograph showing the firehouse facade at left and 3117-3119 Greenmount at right, with 'Ladies/Junior' fascia text and 'NEW ISSUE' legible on the first-floor glazing.

Doris Engelman Dogoloff, Paul Engelman's widow who had remarried Mark Dogoloff after Paul's 1976 death, died and was remembered as 'beloved wife of the late Paul Engelman and the late Mark Dogoloff, beloved mother of Peter G. and Jerry R. Engelman.'

In a condolence comment on the Legacy.com obituary page for Irene Catherine Barker (nee Arndt, 1918-2013), Peter G. Engelman recalled that Barker had worked as bookkeeper and salesfloor employee for his father's toy store on Greenmount Avenue, especially at Christmas.

Irene Catherine Barker (nee Arndt), who had worked as bookkeeper and salesfloor employee for Paul Engelman's toy store at 3117 Greenmount, died September 27, 2013 at age 95 in Timonium, Maryland, with interment at Druid Ridge Cemetery.

The Waverly Main Street Historic District (B-5229), roughly 31 acres and 143 contributing buildings along Greenmount Avenue between East 29th and East 35th Streets, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 31, 2013, with 3117 Greenmount Avenue identified as a contributing two-story commercial building on Block 4076A, Lot 014.

Nam Seo Koo and Seon Gyu Koo conveyed the property to 3117 Greenmount Avenue, LLC for $380,000, executed February 16, 2017 (notarized February 14, 2017), and recorded March 2, 2017, establishing the building's current ownership.
3117 Greenmount Avenue, LLC, acting as guarantor, executed an Indemnity Deed of Trust securing a $1,500,000 loan to borrower Nirav Babu, executed November 14, 2017 and recorded January 19, 2018.

George W. Coffield, described as 'Afro-American,' died January 12, 1918, memorialized by his widow Louise Coffield in a February 1924 In Memoriam notice. The white paper flags an open question as to whether this is the same person as the 1865 grantee George C. H. Coffield.
Louise Coffield published an In Memoriam notice in the Afro-American remembering her late husband George W. Coffield, who had died January 12, 1918.
The Waverly Fire House at 3123 Greenmount Avenue, the dominant structure on the block and 3117's near neighbor to the north, was built in 1900-1901; it was rehabilitated in 2009-2010.

The Provident Savings Bank Waverly branch building at 3111 Greenmount Avenue, immediately adjacent to 3117, was built ca. 1925, bringing working-class neighborhood-branch banking (Provident had been chartered in 1886) directly onto the block.

Louis Rabai (b. Italy ~1902-03) came to the United States in 1923 to join his brother, John B. Rabai, in the baking business. About a decade later he went into business for himself — the bakery he ran on Greenmount Avenue.

Rabai's Bakery, an Art Deco shop, opened at 3215 Greenmount Ave in 1937, run by Louis Rabai. A neighborhood retail bakery ('For Those Who Want the Best') known for coconut sticks, meringue pies, gingerbread cookies and peach cake.

A mid-century Rabai's Bakery matchbook (Maryland Match Co.) advertises the slogan 'For Those Who Want the Best' and two locations: 3215 Greenmount Ave (University 5800) and 5110 Park Heights Ave (Liberty 4880) — a two-store retail bakery.
Louis Rabai ran his Greenmount Avenue bakery until he sold it in 1952, after roughly two decades of ownership.

After Louis Rabai sold the Greenmount shop (1952), it is reported operating by the mid-1950s as 'Burri's French Bakery' — 'Burri' almost certainly the Brusini family name (the co-founding branch, related to the Rabais by the Vicarini-sisters marriages) continuing the bakery before its later Butter Crisp era.

Michael Gotti incorporated Butter Crisp Bakery, Inc. at 3215 Greenmount Ave on March 21, 1977 (MD entity D00740985; Articles of Incorporation Film F2378/Folio 461), taking over the former Rabai's/Burri's storefront and continuing the parcel's ~50 years of bakery use. Gotti (an Italian surname; home at 5900 Benton Heights Rd, NE Baltimore) was the resident agent/proprietor. The bakery hired an 'all-around baker, morning shift' in 1978 and advertised through the 1980s. (Michael Gotti the baker is thinly documented — no obituary or grave found online, and he is NOT the New York crime-family John Gotti.)

Butter Crisp Bakery (the former Rabai's) closed around 1987, one of many 'Avenue' store closings in the 1980s that triggered community concern. The corporation's Maryland charter was formally FORFEITED on Oct 11, 1989 (~2 years after the shop stopped operating).

3215 Greenmount today is Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart. The 1938 Art Deco storefront documented in the BG&E photos — curved-glass entrance, the 'RABAI'S BAKERY' blade sign, stepped parapet — is gone, replaced by a plain modern retrofit; only the brick shell survives (a 'contributing resource' in the Waverly Main Street Historic District). The consolidated parcel is recorded under 3213 (Block 4076 Lot 7).

Louis Rabai, 'long the proprietor of a bakery [on] Greenmount avenue' and 'a leader in the Italo-American community,' died at 54 after a long illness. He came from Italy in 1923 to join his brother John B. Rabai in baking, went into business for himself ~1933, and sold his shop in 1952. He served ten years (three terms) on the Baltimore City Jail Board and was for a time chairman of Italy's own Boys Town in Rome.

Mary Vicarini Rabai, who with her husband John B. Rabai ran a series of businesses called Rabai's French Bakery (downtown stores supplying French bread and hard dinner rolls to restaurants), died at 93. Born in Paris in 1896 to Italian parents, she came to Baltimore's Little Italy at age 8 and married John B. Rabai in 1914. Their children included Ermine (DePasquale) — pictured working at the Greenmount store in 1938 — Edith Segraves, and Cmdr. John F. Rabai. (The Rabai's French Bakery was the family's downtown/wholesale line, distinct from Louis Rabai's Greenmount retail shop.)

Baltimore Gas & Electric photographed the Art Deco storefront and window displays of Rabai's Bakery on Greenmount Avenue on Feb 3, 1938 — documenting the Moderne shopfront (curved glass, illuminated blade sign) at the time of an electrical modernization.

Three BG&E interior views of Rabai's Bakery on Greenmount Ave (Feb 3, 1938) show women in white behind glazed-tile display cases full of baked goods; the catalog names Ermine Rabai (daughter of John B. & Mary Rabai) at the store.

The bakery family had TWO men named Louis, often conflated: (1) Louis RABAI (b.1902 Italy, immigrated 1923 to join his brother John, ran the Greenmount store, City Jail Board, d. Mar 14 1957) — buried New Cathedral Cemetery Plot VV-714, beside brother John B. Rabai (1896-1961) at VV-704; and (2) Louis BRUSINI, who married Rosa Vicarini (sister of John's wife Mary), making him John's brother-in-law and bakery co-founder. John B. Rabai m. Mary Vicarini (b. Paris 1896, d.1990) in 1914; their children were Ermine (DePasquale), Edith (Segraves), and John Frank Rabai (1921-2013, ran the bakery after WWII). Living descendants include grandson Peter DePasquale (Ermine's son) and Amy Brusini. A charming coda: the widowed Mary Rabai sailed on the RMS Caronia's Mediterranean cruise from New York on May 6, 1965.

Rabai's Bakery was founded in the 1920s by Louis (Luigi) Brusini and his brother-in-law John B. Rabai — the two men had married the Vicarini sisters (John m. Mary Vicarini 1914; Louis Brusini m. Rosa Vicarini 1918). The original location was on Edmondson Avenue in West Baltimore; the business grew to multiple stores, including the Greenmount Avenue retail bakery (run by John's brother Louis Rabai) and a Park Heights Ave branch.

In Waverly memory Rabai's was a beloved fixture a couple of doors from the Waverly Theater (near Zales): people stopped after church or after a movie. Remembered for yeast doughnuts, sticky pecan buns, crumb cake, milk bread, coconut sticks, meringue pies, and a peach cake called 'the unofficial taste of Baltimore summers.' A neighborhood boy traded his Morning Sun paper for a bun at the back door; delivery driver Jim Frizzera brought fresh rolls to the neighbors. 'Some of the nicest people in the world.'

A Baltimore Sun marriage-license listing records Luigi Brusini, of Brentwood Avenue, marrying Rosa Vicarini, age 20 — the union that made Louis Brusini brother-in-law to John B. Rabai (who had married Rosa's sister Mary Vicarini in 1914) and a co-founder of Rabai's Bakery.

After the Rabai's/Burri's bakery era, the same storefront at 3215 Greenmount Avenue carried on as the Butter Crisp Bakery (incorporated 1977 under Michael Gotti). A July 3, 1978 Evening Sun help-wanted ad — 'BAKER. All around, morning shift, apply in person only. Butter Crisp Bakery, 3215 Greenmount Ave.' — confirms it operated at Rabai's exact address and was actively hiring its own bakers. Butter Crisp has a substantial newspaper footprint (~39 Baltimore Sun/Evening Sun matches), running from 1978 through a cluster of mentions in September 1987 (its apparent closing, amid the wave of 1980s Avenue store closings that alarmed the community) and a final trace into July 1988 — roughly a decade at the corner before the storefront's later conversion (today Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart, the Art Deco front lost).
In 1920 the flat above/behind the Keyes grocery housed Robert L. Ward, a plasterer, after the Keyes family themselves moved to 2952 Greenmount — a typical mixed store-and-lodging corner.
By 1930-1936 the independent Keyes grocery had given way to an American Stores Co. chain grocery at 3201 Greenmount — the corner's shift from independent to chain retail.

A late-1930s streetscape photograph of the Greenmount & E 32nd St node (the Old York Rd wedge) captures the commercial cluster 3201's corner store anchored. Legible businesses include a White Coffee Pot restaurant, the Family Finance Corporation, Brandau's / 'Marlboro' Clothes, and a W.L. Douglas 'Cinderella Shoe Shop' selling Weather Bird Shoes, with a large HEINZ OVEN-BAKED BEANS billboard mounted atop the corner building. On the sidewalk at the corner stands an open-air fruit-and-flower stand — crates of produce and potted flowers — the kind of outdoor display the 3201 corner grocery ran. A 1960s color view of the same stretch shows the block's later tenants (Nifty Cleaners, Roberts Jewelers) with the Waverly Theatre marquee and a streetcar beyond.

The mid-to-late-20th-century owner of 3201 Greenmount was Matthew Swerdloff, a colorful Baltimore figure. Reared in Forest Park, he graduated City College (1944, lacrosse attackman), took a B.A. (1952) and law degree (1955) at the University of Baltimore, played lacrosse there (1952 North-South Game at NY's Polo Grounds, All-American honorable mention). In 1958-59 he was GENERAL MANAGER of the (Eastern Basketball League) Baltimore Bullets — a struggling minor-league pro basketball team he kept afloat by scrounging backers, doing front-office work unpaid while practicing law (the club ran ~$15,000 in the red, drew 500-600 fans a game, sat 6th at 7-11). He was also head coach of the Maryland Lacrosse Club and became a legendary lacrosse referee ('the Charley Eckman of lacrosse') — refereeing 1953-73 and 1986-95, president of the Southern Lacrosse Officials Assn, co-founder of the National Intercollegiate Lacrosse Officials Assn, teacher of youth lacrosse at the JCC (1960), and founder of the Heroes summer lacrosse leagues (1965) that gave players scholarships. He later worked in real estate (owning this Greenmount corner). A Mount Washington resident, he died Feb 25, 1995 (age 64) of a heart attack while refereeing a scrimmage at Anne Arundel Community College; his estate sold 3201 in July 1996.

3201 Greenmount today is the Greenmount / 'GM' Tobacco Outlet, a tobacco/convenience specialty store (owned by the Koo family, leased to the operator) — matching the 2026 police report's 'specialty store' robbery and a food-facility complaint at the address.

William F. Keyes — the corridor's 3201 Greenmount corner grocer (or his same-named son) — died June 5, 1963, by then a resident of Stevenson, MD (an affluent Baltimore County suburb), a marker of the modest immigrant-grocer family's upward path off the Avenue.
