The E 32nd St corner. The odd (east) 3200 block is the WAVERLY THEATRE block on the old York Rd frontage; in 1915 the map carries dual numbers (new Greenmount + old York Rd ~1109-1115), by 1928 only Greenmount numbers remain.

Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps (1915 / 1928 / 1953) for 3203 Greenmount: a brick storefront in front of the block's 'Picture Show/Billiards' (1915) -> brick store (1928) -> a SIGN-PRINTING shop by 1953. The Deal family confectionery/soda-water storefront. The odd (east) 3200 block is the WAVERLY THEATRE block on the old York Rd frontage; in 1915 the map carries dual numbers (new Greenmount + old York Rd ~1109-1115), by 1928 only Greenmount numbers remain.

Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps (1915 / 1928 / 1953) for 3211 Greenmount: the block's 'Picture Show & Billiards' building (1915) -> the WAVERLY THEATRE (moving pictures) by 1928/1953 -> reinforced with steel beams by 1953. The theatre auditorium ran back behind the storefronts. The odd (east) 3200 block is the WAVERLY THEATRE block on the old York Rd frontage; in 1915 the map carries dual numbers (new Greenmount + old York Rd ~1109-1115), by 1928 only Greenmount numbers remain.

Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps (1915 / 1928 / 1953) for 3213 Greenmount: part of the Picture Show/Billiards building (a 3-story brick front) in 1915 -> the WAVERLY THEATRE ENTRANCE by 1928/1953 -- immediately beside Rabai's Bakery's storefront (the bakery and the theatre entrance shared this stretch). The odd (east) 3200 block is the WAVERLY THEATRE block on the old York Rd frontage; in 1915 the map carries dual numbers (new Greenmount + old York Rd ~1109-1115), by 1928 only Greenmount numbers remain.

Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps (1915 / 1928 / 1953) for 3217 Greenmount: a FRAME 2-story DWELLING in 1915 -> converted to a brick 2-story STORE (with a show window) by 1928, still a store in 1953 -- the block's dwelling-to-store commercialization. The odd (east) 3200 block is the WAVERLY THEATRE block on the old York Rd frontage; in 1915 the map carries dual numbers (new Greenmount + old York Rd ~1109-1115), by 1928 only Greenmount numbers remain.

Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps (1915 / 1928 / 1953) for 3221 Greenmount: a brick 2-story STORE (spanning 3221-3223, ~24 ft) through 1915-1953 (skylights added by 1953). The odd (east) 3200 block is the WAVERLY THEATRE block on the old York Rd frontage; in 1915 the map carries dual numbers (new Greenmount + old York Rd ~1109-1115), by 1928 only Greenmount numbers remain.

Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps (1915 / 1928 / 1953) for 3223 Greenmount: a brick 2-story corner STORE in 1915 -> by 1953 a DRUGSTORE ('Drugs'); a paint-cleaner manufacturer operated at its rear (#509) in 1928. The odd (east) 3200 block is the WAVERLY THEATRE block on the old York Rd frontage; in 1915 the map carries dual numbers (new Greenmount + old York Rd ~1109-1115), by 1928 only Greenmount numbers remain.

Before the Greenmount renumbering, 3217 was 1113 York Road, home to the O'Brien family: Charles H. O'Brien (a printer, also listed as a mariner), James T. O'Brien (driver), and James T. O'Brien Jr. — listed as a JOCKEY — plus, by 1909, John H. Dietrich.
In 1915, 3217 Greenmount was still a frame 2-story dwelling (per Sanborn), home to Harry R. McAllister, a plumber, and Mrs. Alice A. Akers — before it became a hardware store.

James W. McClellan (with wife Annie) ran a HARDWARE store at 3217 Greenmount from ~1918 through the early 1920s — the use that converted the old frame dwelling into the brick storefront (Sanborn shows it brick by 1928). The McClellans lived off-site (319 E ...).

The Waverly Theatre at 3211 Greenmount Ave opened in 1909 as a neighborhood movie house, designed by architect Alfred 'A.' Lowther Forrest in partnership with Oliver Birkhead Wight. Its façade was a classical temple-style front with a large arched window and a decorative 'W' monogram — a scaled-down echo of the Beaux-Arts elegance the pair brought to Baltimore's downtown picture palaces. The Waverly is the project that ties Forrest and Wight together; its success led to Wight's involvement in their subsequent commissions. The building survives today as a retail store, still recognizable by its original theatre front.

Alfred Lowther Forrest was born 1862 in Notting Hill, London, trained in architecture in London from age 19, and emigrated to the U.S. in 1898 (Boston/New York) before settling in Baltimore by 1907 — a city rebuilding after the 1904 Great Fire. He briefly worked for Baldwin & Pennington (B&O Railroad architects) before opening his own North Charles St office. A prolific theatre architect — 'he designed more than a dozen theaters, most of them in Baltimore' (Headley) — his works include the Victoria/Embassy Theatre (1908), the New Theatre (1910, co-designed with Wight), the Second-Empire Macht Building (1908, an early post-fire landmark), and Roland Avenue M.E. Church (1912). He left Baltimore for Rochester, NY ca.1928 and died in 1951, age 89.

Oliver Birkhead Wight was a Baltimore-born architect (b. ca.1876–1880) who became one of the city's principal theatre designers of the 1910s–1930s. His early collaboration with Forrest on the Waverly (1909) and the New Theatre (1910) gave him his start in cinema architecture; by 1915 he was a registered AIA architect. His masterpiece was the Parkway Theatre (1915), modeled on London's West End and now restored as the SNF Parkway Film Center in Station North. He also remodeled the Howard Theatre (1920), designed the Arcade (1928) and Avon (1933) in Hamilton, the Irvington (1925), and the Carroll Theatre in Westminster (now the Carroll Arts Center) — collectively shaping Baltimore's neighborhood-cinema landscape.

The corner lot known as 3201 Greenmount Ave was assembled out of parts of three abutting ground-rent leases granted by Matilda W. Sanger, the ground-rent owner of the block: to William L. Fink (May 27, 1889, Liber J.B. 1244 folio 245), to Charles W. Kraemer & wife (Oct 29, 1892, Liber J.B. 1422 folio 515), and to John N.C. Deal & wife (May 5, 1894, Liber J.B. 1502 folio 284 — folio cited variously as 1504/211 across later documents). Every subsequent deed recites this metes-and-bounds description, which begins 201 ft 1½ in south of the SE corner of Greenmount & Gorsuch Aves and binds on the north side of 32nd St. The three Sanger leases are the deepest recorded root of title for the parcel.

On July 17, 1935 David W. Chertkof & wife conveyed 3201 to John T. Harwood and William Bradford Harwood (undivided ½, joint tenants) and Charles M. Harwood (undivided ½), Liber S.C.L. 5549 folio 267. The Harwood interests then passed by death: John T. Harwood died July 24, 1937, his share vesting in William Bradford Harwood by joint-tenancy survivorship; Charles M. Harwood died Feb 5, 1954, his undivided ½ passing by will (Wills Liber L.C.S. 249/564) to John J. Harwood (who turned 35 on May 30, 1955). The Harwoods held the corner for 21 years.

On June 18, 1956 the Harwoods (John J. & Dorothea Harwood and William Bradford & Jane Harwood) conveyed 3201 to Sol Swerdloff and Anna Swerdloff, his wife, as tenants by the entireties (Liber M.L.P. 10155 folio 100). This is the anchor deed every later instrument recites. Sol Swerdloff later died — the record carries a date conflict: the 1978 mortgage states 'October 6, 1966,' while the 1981/1983/1987/1989/1996 instruments all state 'on or about October 2, 1965.' On his death Anna Swerdloff became sole owner by survivorship. Both death dates are preserved here rather than silently resolved.

Between 1978 and 1982 Anna Swerdloff mortgaged 3201 to secure the businesses of her son Matthew K. Swerdloff (later the parcel's owner and a former Baltimore Bullets GM). A $45,000 Indemnity Mortgage to Citizens National Bank of Laurel (Sept 29, 1978, Liber RHB 3668/488) secured Matthew's 'College Park Connection.' Two Indemnity Deeds of Trust followed on June 4, 1981 (Liber CWM Jr. 4058/787 for $22,500 and 4058/799 for $7,500), both securing 'Pizza Connection, Inc.' A Nov 17, 1982 UCC financing statement (CWM Jr. 4253/592, $60,000 to Union Trust) names tenant 'Greg's Shoes' — Gregory & Deborah Schneider — operating a shoe store at 3201. All were later released (1987). These filings map the corner's commercial tenants and the Swerdloff family's food-service ventures.

On Jan 15, 1988 Anna Swerdloff (by Matthew Swerdloff, her attorney-in-fact) contracted to sell 3201 to Kew Hoea Koo and Sung Hee Koo for $180,000 — $50,000 down and $130,000 seller-financed at 12% over 15 years, buyers taking possession Jan 18, 1988, property sold 'As Is,' zoned B-2-3 (Liber SEB 1617/485, recorded Feb 18, 1988). The contract included a 1996 title survey (Kile, File 76-121) showing a 2-story brick, a 3-story brick, a storefront, two newsstands (one stucco, one frame) and a shed on the lot. This begins the Koo family's long ownership of the corner.

On Feb 28, 1989 Anna Swerdloff (by Matthew, AIF, under a June 17, 1986 power of attorney) deeded 3201 to Matthew Swerdloff and Arlene B. Swerdloff, his wife, as tenants by the entireties, for a nominal $5.00 ('there being no actual consideration'), Liber SEB 2042/370. Matthew Swerdloff subsequently died (Feb 1995), vesting fee simple in Arlene B. Swerdloff by survivorship — setting up her 1996 deed that finally consummated the 1988 Koo contract.

A c.1935 photograph of the Waverly's facade shows the theatre at the height of its neighborhood-movie-house era: the ornate vertical 'WAVERLY' blade sign and chevron marquee reading 'SPENCER TRACY / DANTE INFERNO' (the Fox film Dante's Inferno was released 1935), with a banner urging 'BRING THE CHILDREN to our Special Children's Matinee — Every Saturday at 10 AM.' The theatre is flanked by an A&P grocery on one side and a store ('CROWN') with a striped awning on the other — the tight Waverly commercial row. This is the best surviving image of the 1930s facade with its original signage intact.

A weekly printed program headed 'BOULEVARD AND WAVERLY THEATRES,' Vol. 7, No. 9, Sunday February 23, 1941, shows the Waverly was programmed jointly with the nearby Boulevard Theatre (one block north on Greenmount) under a single operator/circuit. The featured attractions were MGM's 'Flight Command' (Robert Taylor, Ruth Hussey, Walter Pidgeon) and 'Road Show' (Adolphe Menjou, Carole Landis, John Hubbard). The 'Vol. 7' masthead means the joint program had been running weekly since ~1934. (Copy held by the Maryland Department, Enoch Pratt Free Library.)

A 1963 photograph shows the Waverly running the AIP release 'X: The Man with the X-Ray Eyes' (Ray Milland), billed on the marquee as 'MAN WITH THE X-RAY EYES / SPECTARAMA & COLOR' — with a Baltimore PCC streetcar passing on Greenmount Avenue in front of the theatre. The film opened in 1963, the final year of Baltimore streetcar service, dating the image precisely. It captures the Waverly still operating as a first-run neighborhood house into the early 1960s.

By the 1980s the Waverly had closed as a theatre and its front converted to retail — a 'SHOE CITY / The Family Shoe Store' occupied the storefront. Per a kilduffs.com account, the decorative 'W' was still visible atop the building into the 1980s before a new coat of siding hid it; the building's front remained 'easy to spot,' and the old sloped theatre floor survived in the stockroom. A new food store was later built in the rear of the old theatre. The Waverly was remembered as the neighborhood's favorite movie house, one block south of the more upscale Boulevard Theatre.

The original 1909 iron-front picture-show-and-billiards was extensively renovated in 1919 and reopened in 1921 under the name 'the New Waverly Theatre.' The rebuilt brick-and-concrete house seated more than 1,300 people and featured a gold fiber screen and a five-piece orchestra to accompany the pictures — a major upgrade from the storefront nickelodeon. The reopening coincided with the 1919 opening of the Olmsted-designed 33rd Street boulevard and the 1921 debut of the rival, larger Boulevard Theatre three blocks north; the Waverly remained the smaller neighborhood 'community theatre' while the Boulevard drew the Guilford/Peabody Heights crowd.

In the decades before air conditioning, theatres commonly closed in the summer heat. Waverly manager Harry Kahn worked around this by creating an open-air theatre in the open lot behind the building — a bed-sheet screen, wooden folding chairs, and a piano player — so the Waverly could keep showing pictures through the summer. A small, human detail of how a neighborhood movie house survived the season.

Like the other movie theatres on Greenmount Avenue, the Waverly operated under racial segregation for much of its life. The National Register nomination notes the pointed contrast that while the Avenue's movie theatres were segregated, its 'refined stores' were open to everyone and employed Black workers — a marker of the everyday geography of Jim Crow in a mixed commercial district. Part of the corridor's civil-rights-era social record.

The Waverly Theatre — the first theatre in Waverly village, running from silent films through talkies — closed in 1969 after sixty continuous years (1909–1969). The building was converted to commercial retail ca.1970 and given a sheet-metal facade ca.1990; the decorative 'W' that long survived on the parapet was covered over. Part of the building had also housed the Knockblock (Knowblock) Brothers' grocery store (1937), and the storefront later became Shoe City, with today's Raven Grocery & Dollar Mart occupying the space. The terrazzo paving of the former ticket booth still survives at street level (at the 3203 entrance bay).

The National Register nomination records that the 3203 Greenmount building (a ca.1890 2-story commercial building) was part of the Waverly Theatre complex, with terrazzo paving at street level that still reflects the outline of the theatre's former ticket booth. This places the theatre's entrance/lobby at the 3203 bay, with the 1,300-seat auditorium extending back through the adjoining lots (the vanished 3205–3209 storefronts) to the 3211 parcel — explaining how the theatre absorbed Block 4076 lots 004/005. A rare survival of the movie house's physical fabric.

The 3203 (3203-3209) frontage traces through the same amusement-company root as the theatre next door: Crystal Amusement Company → The Grand Company (Nov 30 1929, SCL 5069/562), with a 1955 strip from Beulah Bruehl (MLP 10007/357). It also shares the 1956 Harwood→Sol Swerdloff anchor deed (MLP 10155/100, the same deed that governs 3201). By 1979 Minrose Realty Corp conveyed to Cora Marie Fannin (WA 3732/830); Eli & Yetta Miller then assembled five lots and on Dec 18 1980 conveyed them to The Miller Realty Corporation (CWM Jr. 4025/301), consolidating the 3203-3209 storefronts into one holding.

On Dec 23 1981 The Miller Realty Corporation (Alvin Miller, VP) gave an Indemnity Second Deed of Trust to The Savings Bank of Baltimore (Osmond & Sheffield, Trustees) for $150,000, securing a loan to the retail tenant 'The Princess Shops, Inc.' (CWM Jr. 4142/483). The financing stack layered a $125,000 SBA loan (Small Business Investment Act §503) and a $75,000 City of Baltimore / DHCD loan (CWM Jr. 4142/500) whose proceeds were expressly 'applied to the rehabilitation of properties known as Nos. 3202-05-07-09 Greenmount Avenue.' A documented instance of public urban-renewal money rebuilding a Greenmount retail block.

The Waverly Theatre parcel's chain of title opens with a Matilda W. Sanger ground lease dated Oct 27 1909 to the WAVERLY AMUSEMENT COMPANY (SCL 2537/193) — a deed-record confirmation of the theatre's 1909 founding. It passed to the CRYSTAL AMUSEMENT COMPANY in 1922 (SCL 3844/65, the era of the 1919-21 'New Waverly' rebuild) and on Nov 30 1929 to THE GRAND COMPANY (SCL 5069/562) — the theatre-operating enterprise of Frank H. Durkee III, whose Durkee circuit also ran the nearby Boulevard, explaining the jointly-printed 'Boulevard and Waverly Theatres' programs. In 1955 Beulah Bruehl conveyed a strip to Grand Co (MLP 10007/357) and Grand Co granted a revocable license to the adjoining CROWN 5-AND-10-CENT-TO-$1.00 STORES, INC. (MLP 10007/361) — the Crown store that appears beside the theatre in 1930s photographs.

The combined 3213-3215 parcel traces to a May 21 1884 deed from Leonard Brickhead to Matilda W. Sanger for the whole lot (Baltimore County Liber WMI 141/244) — Sanger appearing here as fee owner, the same matriarch behind the block's ground-rent leases. A second, adjoining lot (shared party walls) was conveyed by Matilda W. Sanger to Mary K. Find and Nellie Grace Holmes on April 28 1913 (SCL 2814/546). The two lots, joined through party walls, became 'Nos. 3213-15 Greenmount Avenue.'

The 3217-3219 parcel (Block 4076, Lot 008; north party wall on the Robert Garonzik property, south references the Edna May Knoblock lot) was conveyed by the Fries 2003 Trust to 3217 Greenmount, LLC on March 23 2009 (FMC 11535/33). The LLC (Quyen Vinh Hau, member) carried a 2012 MDPA H Capital mortgage (released 2013), a 2014 Chesapeake Bank of Maryland / Rosedale IDOT, and a Dec 10 2021 Open Bank Indemnity Deed of Trust for $2,975,000 (Book 24423/166) securing a term loan to QT HAU, LLC — with borrowers Lux Nail Spa & Hair Salon LLC and Hau Realty LLC. Lux Nail Spa & Hair Salon is the operating tenant of the storefront.

The 3221 chain reaches back to a July 23 1919 deed, Clinton E. Stevens → Jacob D. Silverstein (SCL 3411/225), cited for the east party-wall boundary. Alan Wurtzburger conveyed to his wife Janet E. C. Wurtzburger on June 1 1945 (MLP 6751/585); Janet — of the Baltimore art-collecting Wurtzburger family — died Dec 24 1973 (Baltimore County Wills JLD 139/631). On March 2 1976 her surviving personal representatives (Jon Alan Wurtzburger and Charles M. Cahn, Jr.) split the parcel, deeding an undivided half each to Jon Alan Wurtzburger (RHB 3350/162) and Margot W. Milch (RHB 3350/165) for $1 apiece.

The 3223 corner (SE corner Greenmount & Gorsuch, Block 4076 Lot 010) was assembled by the Garonzik family across the 1950s: Marion Elliott (unmarried) → Carl & Ada Garonzik, undivided half, Feb 16 1950 (MLP 8011/116); an April 22 1955 Equitable Trust Company quitclaim confirming halves in Roland Garonzik and Carl & Ada Garonzik (MLP 9771/139); and Wheeler Holding Inc. → Roland & Miriam Garonzik, undivided half, June 17 1958 (JFC 384/26). The Garonziks — the same cigar/grocer family established at 3221/3223 — held the corner for a quarter-century.

3223 operated as 'Mr. Nifty Cleaners,' the dry cleaner visible on the corner in 1960s Greenmount streetscape photos (just north of Rabai's Bakery at 3213). Its dry-cleaning history left chlorinated-solvent (perchloroethylene) contamination: on Oct 16 2012 owner Gary Wah and the Maryland Department of the Environment recorded an Environmental Covenant (FMC 14697/310) under MDE's Controlled Hazardous Substance program, governing groundwater use, indoor-air risk, and a sub-slab depressurization/venting system. Earlier, a 2004 Bank of America indemnity deed of trust (Liber 5059/467) had secured a $50,000 guaranty for Wah's operating entity 'Greenmount, Incorporated' (satisfied 2009).

A March 14, 1920 Baltimore Sun notice shows the original Waverly Theater in operation before its 1921 reconstruction: Mary Pickford's 'Heart o' the Hills' (adapted from the John Fox Jr. story) played Wednesday and Thursday, with a special matinee Wednesday at 2 P.M. Documentary proof the picture house was running first-run features on Greenmount a year before the 'New Waverly' reopening.

The primary-source grand-opening ad: 'We take great pleasure in notifying our patrons that the NEW WAVERLY THEATRE, Greenmount Avenue, at Gorsuch, Will Open Monday, February 21 at 6 P.M.' The opening bill was Jack Holt and Lois Wilson in 'Midsummer Madness' plus Larry Semon in 'Schooldays,' followed by a full week (Otis Skinner in 'Kismet,' Lois Weber's 'To Please One Woman,' 'Heliotrope,' Dorothy Phillips, and William Farnum in 'If I Were King'). The ad states 'DAILY PERFORMANCES — CONTINUOUS 2 TO 11 P.M.' and 'ADMISSIONS: MATINEE 11c; EVENINGS 11c AND 17c,' and displays the theatre's ornate 'W' monogram framed by classical columns. This fixes the exact reopening date of the rebuilt house (the NPS-cited '1921' reopening = Feb 21, 1921).

An April 10, 1921 joint display ad pairs the CRYSTAL (528 N. Gay St.) and the WAVERLY (3211 Greenmount Ave.) under one banner — documentary proof that the Crystal Amusement Company operated both houses as a two-theatre circuit, the pre-Durkee equivalent of the later 'Boulevard and Waverly' pairing. The Waverly's week: Winston Churchill's 'The Inside of the Cup' (Mon), Bebe Daniels in 'Oh, Lady, Lady!' (Tue), Allan Dwan's 'The Forbidden Thing' (Wed), Douglas MacLean in 'The Rookie's Return' (Thu), Viola Dana in 'Cinderella's Twin' (Fri), and William Farnum in 'The Scuttlers' (Sat). Corroborates the deed chain: the Crystal Amusement Company (which took the freehold in 1922, SCL 3844/65) was already operating the Waverly by 1921.

A July 23, 1922 Baltimore Sun 'Northeastern District — Waverly' listing shows the New Waverly's weekly bill a year into operation: Lois Wilson in 'Is Matrimony a Failure?' (Mon/Tue), Gladys Walton in 'Second-Hand Rose' (Wed, the popular song adapted to film — 'a little Irish waif in a Jewish family'), Betty Compson in 'Over the Border' (Thu), Agnes Ayres in 'The Ordeal' (Fri), and John Gilbert in 'Gleam o' Dawn' (Sat). Documents the theatre's steady first-run programming in its early New Waverly years (this era also saw Cecil B. DeMille's 'Saturday Night,' Lionel Barrymore's 'Boomerang Bill,' and Wm. S. Hart's 'White Oak' on the Waverly's marquee).

The 3203-3209 storefront frontage of the Waverly Theatre building housed a CROWN 5c & 10c TO $1 STORES — a Baltimore five-and-dime chain outlet at 3207-09 Greenmount Ave, complete with a soda fountain and luncheonette (a Nov 10 1940 Sun help-wanted sought 'experienced young ladies for fountain and luncheonette'). This is the 'CROWN' store that appears beside the Waverly marquee in 1930s photographs; the theatre's owner, The Grand Company, formally licensed the space to 'Crown 5 and 10c to $1.00 Stores, Inc.' by a 1955 revocable license (MLP 10007/361). The Crown chain grew from its Store No. 3 (517-19 York Road, Towson, pictured in a 1940 'GROWING!' ad as of 1932) to at least six Baltimore-area locations by 1950 — 3207 Greenmount, 735 Washington Blvd, 517 York Rd (Towson), 5436 York Rd, 5118 Park Heights Ave, and Park Lane Shopping Center — open Monday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday evenings.

By 1963 the Crown five-and-dime had wound down here: a Circuit Court trustee's sale in the matter of the Trust Estate of Crown 5c & 10c to $1.00 Stores, Inc. auctioned the property Monday, September 23, 1963. The Greenmount piece was described as '3203-3205-3207-3209 Greenmount Ave.' — a 2-story brick business property with 3 stores and separate-entrance offices above, fronting ~70 feet on Greenmount with an average depth of 175 feet and 'running from Greenmount Avenue to Old York Road' (a through-lot spanning the wedge between the two streets), zoned 1st commercial. Stores at 3203 and 3207-9 were rented ($10,200/yr gross); 3205 and the upstairs offices were vacant. The SAME trust estate also owned a separate property five miles north — 507-509-511 York Road in Towson (Baltimore County), leased to a well-known tenant — sold at the same auction. (The two 'York Road/Greenmount' addresses are the same historic road by lineage but different places: Greenmount Ave is the straightened city segment of the old York Turnpike, with 'Old York Road' surviving as the fork behind the 3200 block; the Towson store is a wholly separate location.) The Greenmount frontage later passed to Eli & Yetta Miller / The Miller Realty Corporation and the 1981 Princess Shops rehab.

The Greenmount storefront was not just a Crown branch — it was the CHAIN'S ORIGIN. A full-page Aug 27, 1936 Evening Sun ad narrating 'THE STORY OF CROWN STORES' opens with 'CHAPTER ONE — The First Crown Store — 3207-09 Greenmount Ave.,' followed by Chapter Two (735-37 Washington Blvd), Chapter Three (517-19 York Rd, Towson — the 1932 'Store No. 3'), and Chapter Four, the newest unit being opened that night at 5118-20 Park Heights Ave ('The Ten-Cent Store Beautiful'). Crown billed itself as 'Maryland's Own Chain — Owned and Operated by Marylanders.' So the corridor birthed a homegrown Baltimore five-and-dime chain: from this 3207-09 Greenmount flagship (c.1930, predating the 1932 Towson store) the chain grew to four stores by 1936 and at least six by 1950. Crown's trust ultimately owned the entire 3203-3209 frontage before auctioning it in 1963.

Rabai's Bakery's earliest documented Greenmount location was 3205 Greenmount Ave — a few doors south of its later signature Art Deco store at 3213-3215. In the Aug 27, 1936 full-page 'welcome Crown' ad, Rabai's ran a congratulation notice giving both its addresses: '3205 Greenmount Ave. / 5110 Park Heights Ave. — Near the Crown.' Rabai's shadowed the Crown chain at both ends: a Greenmount store beside the first Crown (3207-09) and a Park Heights store beside Crown's new 1936 unit (5118-20). By 1937-38 Rabai's operated from the purpose-built Art Deco storefront at 3213-3215 Greenmount (the BMI 1938 photographs; the 'For Those Who Want the Best' matchbook, '3215 Greenmount + 5110 Park Heights') — so 3205 was an early location and the move north to 3213-3215 came ~1937.

As the chain's founding store, 3207 Greenmount doubled as Crown's hiring office and headquarters. A long run of Baltimore Sun / Evening Sun help-wanted ads placed from '3207 Greenmount Ave.' (phone UNiversity 6880) recruited for the whole chain — an Aug 27 1941 ad sought 'young ladies… selling positions open in our various stores… Apply Miss Stricker' (naming the store's hiring manager); others sought receiving/stockroom young men (1941), a store manager and stock man (1943), 'girls 16 or over' to 'earn Xmas money… in your own neighborhood' (1943), window trimmers (1944), and sign-holders (1948). A Sept 1943 ad's segregated 'Porters — Colored. Steady work' reflects the era's Jim Crow hiring language. By Oct 1958 the firm advertised as the incorporated 'Crown 5c & 10c to $1 Stores, Inc.' of 'Baltimore 18, Maryland,' a self-described 'rapidly expanding chain' hiring assistant managers — 3207 Greenmount still its address.

On the night of Nov 25, 1951, burglars used a 4-pound maul to batter open the large second-floor office safe at Rabai's Bakery, 3215 Greenmount Avenue, and escaped with $3,320 in cash — the noise drowned out by the dough-mixing machinery running in the basement as the bakers worked below. Owner Louis Rabai told police the thieves also took a solid gold cigarette lighter ($240) and a $300 pocket watch, and drank a bottle of the bakery's brandy (kept for use in the recipes). The robbers had scaled a light pole in the side alley, forced the second-floor window of chiropodist Dr. Jacob Ostroff, and crossed into the Rabai office; the break-in was discovered the next morning by attorney J. Philip Knapp, whose office was nearby. Sgt. Allen Berman of the Northeastern district investigated. A press photo shows 'Louis Rabai inspects battered safe in his bakery.'

The proprietor of Rabai's Bakery was a fixture of Baltimore's Italian-American civic and political world. Louis Rabai chaired the arrangements committee of the Italian-American Civic Club of Maryland — organizing its Columbus Day banquet in Oct 1945 (with Anselm Sodaro as club president) and standing among the Little Italy families who feted Mayor Tommy D'Alesandro at the club's 1947 testimonial dinner. In July 1947 Mayor D'Alesandro appointed Rabai to the Baltimore City Jail Board (term to July 1, 1951), on which he served, through reappointment in 1955, until his death — a tenure that included the board's March 1957 vote to desegregate the jail's visiting system (removing the Jim Crow sign). He was also the 'third man' in the uncropped photograph State's Attorney Anselm Sodaro used to defend himself in the bitter 1954 primary. Rabai's Bakery itself made a wartime Red Cross War Fund honor roll of organizations that exceeded their campaign goals.

Louis Rabai died March 14, 1957, of 5305 St. Albans Way, husband of Pauline A. Rabai (née Ciotti); his Requiem Mass was at St. Mary's Church, Govans, and the Italian American Civic Club of Maryland (Julius A. Romano, president) noted his passing. A brother, John B. Rabai, was the bakery's corporate face — listed as a director of Traders Savings & Loan Association (1223 W. Baltimore St.) in 1954-56 as 'John B. Rabai, Rabai's Bakery,' and appearing (with daughter Miss Edith Rabai) as the Italian-American representative at the 1954 Baltimore Stewards & Caterers' Club president's ball. The two Rabai brothers, both Italian-American bakers, ran the family bakery business of which 3213-3215 Greenmount was the retail store.

The Rabai family reached into Baltimore's signature sport. John Rabai was one of only two seniors on the 1943 University of Maryland lacrosse team, playing the season finale against Johns Hopkins on May 22, 1943, before leaving for military service upon graduation. A next-generation Rabai in the lacrosse-and-wartime story that runs through the corridor (cf. the Swerdloff and Russell athlete threads).

Bavarian immigrant Jacob Aull (1804-1876) purchased a gravel pit on the west side of the York Turnpike in the 1830s, built a house and opened a cobbler shop — considered the FIRST non-agricultural enterprise in the area (alongside a corn husk depot, a blacksmith, and three small stone houses). Old Land Marks item 2: 'Residence, Late Jacob Aull, 1836; West side York Road, near 31st Street.' NPS B-5229 p51: 'Around the time Waverly became an official community in 1830 a few stores in the hamlet included a blacksmith and a shoemaker's shop owned by Bavarian immigrant Jacob Aull... his sons would go on to build houses during the first construction boom in Waverly.' Wife: Christiana Gusema (1812-1880); five children incl. Louisa Frederika, Margaret Eva, Louis J., Jacob Henry.
Death of Waverly's founding shoemaker, aged ~72. Newspapers.com obituary index: 'Jacob Aull sr., d. Jun 4, 1876, [native of] Bavaria' (Sun 6/27/1876 p4).
Death of Jacob Aull's widow, nee Gusema (b. 1812). Obituary index residence: Waverly.

Old Land Marks item 7: 'Residence Misses M. E. And L. F. Aull, 1895, 3116 York Road; On site of the old Home, west side York Road, near 31st Street.' Louisa Frederika (b. ~1844) and Margaret Eva (b. ~1842), daughters of Jacob & Christiana, replace their father's 1836 cottage with a new house and live there for the next ~47 years. Photo = Old Land Marks item 7.

Louisa F. Aull and Margaret E. Aull (teacher) listed at '3116 York rd' 1901-1909, '3116 Greenmt av' from 1913 (the street renaming visible in the directories). No other surname ever appears at 3116 in the surveyed years.

Verbatim: 'AULL.—On June 28, 1932, MARGARET E., aged 90 years, daughter of the late Jacob H. and Christina S. Aull. Funeral services at her home, 3116 Greenmount avenue, on Thursday at...' (note the obit styles the father 'Jacob H.' — recorded as-is; the founder is usually 'Jacob'). Estate: Orphans' Court letters testamentary granted Oct 1932 (Sun 10/12/1932 p21).

Verbatim: 'AULL.—On February 22, 1942, LOUISA F., age 98 years, beloved daughter of the late Jacob and Christianna Aull. Funeral services will be at her home, 3116 Greenmount avenue, on Tuesday at 2 P.M. Interment in...' The last Aull leaves the ground the family had held since 1836 — 106 years.

NPS B-5229 p24: 3114/3116 Greenmount is a '1-story commercial building built ca. 1955' (non-contributing; later the Red Shed), and 'was historically the site of the residence of M.E. and L.F. Aull.' The 3116 address disappears from the parcel fabric — which is why this history attaches to today's 3114.

Joe Stewart (2019): 'Included in the photos is one I took inside Huntingdon Baptist of a window in memory of the two Aull sisters who lived around the corner from and attended that church.' Dating of the window installation not yet established.

Old Land Marks item 5: 'Residence Louis J. Aull, 1888, 414 Waverly Avenue; Louis J. Aull, Shop, 3101 Talbott Street.' Louis J. Aull, carpenter/builder son of shoemaker Jacob, was with brother Jacob H. one of the two Aull developers who 'transformed the country hamlet into a suburban village.' Polk situates the shop 'Talbott nr Waverly av' (1905) / 'Talbott nr Gilmor la' (1909); by 1918 the Waverly Garage occupied 3100 Talbott. Waverly Ave was renamed E 31st St (directories flip by 1915).

Louis J. Aull's wife was Kate R. Aull nee Reynolds (per her 1930 death notice) — the 1909 Reynolds boarder at his house is very likely her kin (or Kate herself as household member). INFERRED, not proven.

Obituary index: Louis Aull, d. Mar 1, 1912, residence 414 East Thirtyfirst street (Evening Sun 3/1/1912 p12). His widow Kate R. moved to Fair Oak Ave (Polk: 8 Fairoak 1913; 608 Fair Oak 1918-21; 604 Fairoak 1922).

Fredk W. Melis (clerk, householder) with Adeline M. Melis (teacher) and Meissner boarders (Carl F. clk; Otto L. tailor), 1915 through 1923. Later the Thir-Tea First Street Cafe (NPS) and the Old Waverly History Exchange & Tea Room.

Death notice (Sun & Evening Sun 2/28/1930): '...R. (nee Reynolds) beloved wife of the late Louis J. Aull. Funeral from her late residence 604 East 31st street... 1.30 P.M. Interment in ... Cemetery.' DISCREPANCY: Polk 1922 had her at 604 FAIROAK Ave — either she moved or Fairoak/31st addresses were conflated; both recorded.

Old Land Marks item 26: 'Waverly Hall, 1872... York Road and 31st Street.' NPS B-5229 p49: built 1873, 'partially on property originally owned by the shoemaker, Jacob Aull'; Scharf: 'a spacious brick building, sixty by a hundred feet' with library, used for public meetings, lectures, fairs, balls; Maryland State Senate commemorated its centennial in 1973 (implying 1873). DATE CONFLICT 1872 vs 1873 recorded, not resolved.

Old Land Marks item 26 names 'Nome Progressive Castle No. 20' and 'Baltimore Temple No. 1 Knights and Ladies Golden Eagle' at Waverly Hall. Polk 1913-1918 add Waverly Conclave No 57 (IOH), Waverly Council (Jr OUAM), Temple No 1 & Castle No 20 (K.G.E.). Mary Ann Jessup Clemens Aull — Jacob H. Aull's second wife — was Grand Deputy for Maryland of the Ladies of the Golden Eagle (stuffctwfound): the Aull family on both the deed and the lodge rolls.

Clemens Bros (Lennox B. & Augustus D.) auto accessories at 3019 York Rd/Greenmount 1913-15, then 'Clemens A D jr Sons, real est, 422 e 31st' (1918) / '428 e 31st n' (1920-22) / 'York rd and 31st n' (1923) — the 1936 rear addition of the Town Hall building carries exactly the 422-428 E 31st addresses. The Clemens family (Better Waverly's developers, Aull in-laws) ran their office from Waverly's civic heart.

Old Land Marks items 8/10: St. John's congregation's first service was held Nov 1843 in 'Part of Old Revolutionary Barracks, formerly in front of St. John's Church.' NPS B-5229 p55: the site originally held a stone barracks housing British soldiers (Revolutionary War and War of 1812), and that adapted barracks was Waverly's FIRST SCHOOL.
Old Land Marks item 10 (Rev. Wm. D. Morgan, Rector era caption).
Old Land Marks item 10. NPS gives 'originally built 1847.'

Old Land Marks item 10: 'Church destroyed by fire, May 15, 1858.' NPS inventory: 're-built after 1858 fire on original walls and foundation, enlarged in 1875'; NPS narrative says 'built in 1859' — internal discrepancy recorded. Parish house 1866, rectory 1868.
Old Land Marks item 9: 'New Gateway St. John's Church, 1905' — photographed for the booklet within a year of construction.

Old Land Marks item 6: 'Waverly M. E. Church, 1871; Rev. A. W. Rudisill; York Road, opposite 31st Street.' NPS B-5229 p20: 3031 Greenmount (now Goodwill) 'was historically the site of a Methodist church... constructed at the 2-mile marker along Old York Road to indicate its distance from City Hall' (Anna Cole). NOTE: the ~1910s BRG12 condemnation plat shows a 'Waverly M.E. Church' lot up on Old York Rd near Montpelier St — likely the congregation's LATER site; two locations recorded, not conflated.

Old Land Marks item 19. NPS B-5229 p15: the school stood at what was 3228 Greenmount — a portion of today's 3240 'Baker Block' (ca. 1925 Mission-style strip); School 51 relocated to 34th St and the site later housed a Woolworth's.

Baltimore County Union transfer column, 9th district: 'Jacob H. Aull & wife to Louisa F. Aull', 'Jacob H. Aull & wife to Maggie E. Aull', 'Lewis J. Aull to Maggie E. Aull.' Nine years after this partition the sisters build the 1895 house at 3116; specific parcels not identified in the column (some conveyances likely include the 32xx lots on the BRG12 plat).

'Hr. Louis J. Aull von Waverly schwer an den Beinen verletzt' — leg injuries in an Atlantic City electric-railway accident. NOTE: a different Louis Aull (downtown coal dealer, 908 Fawn St, also Bavarian-born) died Nov 17, 1909 at 1425 John St (DDC obit 11/21/1909: London Park Cemetery, Turners, Rheinpfalz) — the two men are distinct; OUR Louis J. of 414 E 31st died Mar 1, 1912. Red herring flagged.

Taeglicher Baltimore Wecker timetables (Jun-Sep 1871, verified 7 issues): 'Abgang von Baltimore nach Waverly Hall um 8 Morgens...' (Baltimore & Towsontown line, Henry Tyson, Supt — the same Tyson who named Waverly). Sun 7/19/1871 p1: 'Among the numerous attract[ions is] a fine public hall, erected re[cently at] $12,000.' TOGETHER these contradict both build dates on record (booklet: 1872; CHAP/NPS: 1873) — either the hall predates both claims, or an earlier hall stood at the terminus. Conflict recorded, unresolved.

Fells Point sailmaker-merchant James Biays — commander of the 5th Regimental Cavalry District (Baltimore Hussars) at the Battle of North Point, Sept 12, 1814, scouting the British landings for Gen. Stricker — built his seat 'Mt. Jefferson' on land deeded by Sam Smith as part of 'Ensor's Inspection,' west side of York Rd between today's 29th and 30th; a cupola/roof walk let him 'watch his ships come into port' (visible as the ridge balustrade in the Pratt photograph). Great-grandsons through the Biays line include Mayor J. Barry Mahool (Sun Defenders' Day roster, 9/6/1889 — Mahool born at Phoenix, Balto Co, NOT in this house). Build date circa; Biays death date (commonly 1822) unverified — verify grade.

Old Land Marks item 29: 'Home Late Ex-Mayor Samuel Brady. Now Public School Annex. Formerly occupied by Lieut. Col. James Biays, Great-grandfather of Hon. James Barry Mahool. Gilmor Lane and 29th Street.' Samuel Brady (b. Delaware, d. Dec 8, 1871, aged 82): Gay St dry-goods merchant, Democrat, defeated incumbent Sheppard C. Leakin in 1840, RESIGNED March 1842 in a City Council dispute over the city buying B&O Railroad stock. The 1877 Hopkins atlas labels the parcel 'Samuel Brady Est.' (son Samuel Jr. of Waverly in the patron list); Sun 7/19/1871: 'Before reaching Waverly, a point commonly known as the "first tollgate," is the finely-situated place of Mr. Samuel Brady.' Gilmor Lane = today's Vineyard Lane (MSA street index); Holmes St = E 29th.

Enoch Pratt Maryland Dept photograph (Thomas Chew Worthington III collection, undated, streetcar-era): 'Photograph of the back of the Brady House, located along York Road... later used as the Waverly Public School in the 20th century' — 2.5-story stuccoed Federal house, 5-bay, portico, roof-walk balustrade, windows boarded, grounds unmown. Waverly's school district was No. 51; the booklet says 'Public School Annex' — the word 'annex' and the school number remain UNCONFIRMED by a primary source. OPEN TENSION: this block (29th/Greenmount/30th/Barclay) is the Terrapin/Oriole Park block (1914-1944), yet an MdHS photo shows people at 'the Brady Mansion on York Road' in 1934 — footprint reconciliation unresolved (house may have stood outside the grandstand footprint, or dates need work). Recorded, not resolved.

A 22nd-ward meeting discusses 'opening up Barclay Street parallel to the York Road through the Brady property and the land of Dr. Wilson to Waverly avenue or thirty-fifth street' — the estate consumed by the street grid; the Abell rowhouse fabric follows ~1900+.

Undated 19th-c. clipping (Jeff's data room): 'The commissioners of the Waverly fire department, Mr. A. Hoen, president, have adopted a plan for the department building submitted by J. Appleton Wilson, of Baltimore... truck, ladder and buckets from Wm. & J. H. Leonhardt, of Waverly ($495)... to build the house on the York road, near the tollgate, the lot to be purchased of Mrs. Blum. The building proposed is to contain a lockup in addition to its engine and truck quarters.' (President's name reads 'A. Hoen' vs the MIHP draft's 'A. Boehm' — CONFLICT flagged.) Sun 7/3/1902: 'erected in 1878 by Baltimore county... as a station house and quarters for the old Waverly Volunteer Fire Department, and was later used as quarters for the county chemical engine company [No. 4 Chemical]... Capt. William H. Taylor, of No. 7 Company, was captain of old No. 4 company.' County horses Monte and Baccarat added 1891 (Sun 7/8/1891 p6).

Sun 7/19/1890 p6 ('Fire Department Regulations and Changes'): 'No. 7 hook-and-ladder company is at Waverly, formerly No. 4 hook-and-ladder company.' Both designations then coexist in the one house — Sun 10/20/1900: 'the horses of No. 7 Hook-and-Ladder Company, stationed at No. 4 Chemical Engine House, Waverly, became unmanageable and ran away' (the Mrs. Duncan fire, 212 Reese St; driver Andrew McCormick). Lewis H. Burkhardt appointed driver Nov 3, 1890, rose to deputy chief (obit 11/11/1930). RESOLVES Old Land Marks item 34: 'No. 7 Truck House, 1893' = the 1878 building photographed in 1893 under its post-1890 designation; 'opposite Merryman's Lane' is approximate — no evidence of a separate 1893 building.

Sun 7/3/1902 p7: 'NEW HOME FOR NO. 7 COMPANY — Old House Is Being Torn Down And Handsome One To Be Built' on the SAME site. Sun 3/3/1903 p6: 'No. 7 Hook and Ladder Company, of Waverly, moved into its new quarters yesterday. During the erection of the new building the company has been stationed at the Waverly car barn of the United Railways and Electric Company.' — the car barn that burned three years later. Bronze plaque: '1902, Thomas G. Hayes, Mayor'; city lists say 1901; NPS inventory says 'built 1900-1901' — DATE SPREAD recorded (best form ca. 1901-03). MHT contributing resource B-2788.

Chiefs' reports had urged an engine company 'in the vicinity of York road and Gorsuch avenue' since 1898 (Sun 1/7/1898, 1/10/1900, 1/16/1901; post-fire underwriters' plan 1904-06). Engine 31 organized between 1906 and 1915 (exact date = open gap). Sunday Sun Magazine 8/29/1965 ('The Wonderful Fire Horses of Long Ago,' John C. Treshman): 1915 photo of No. 31's hose wagon 'at Thirty-First street and Greenmount avenue' — Capt. Jim Clark, Lt. Henry Bonner, Jim Savoch at the reins, horses Charlie, Joe and Jim; thirteen horses rotating for hose wagon, No. 7 Ladder Truck and the steamer; harnesses dropped from the ceiling; out 'in a minute or so.' A lieutenant to the whip-happy chief: 'If you ever touch one of my horses with a whip again, I'll kill you!' Eugene F. Daly of Engine 31 started the Fire Department's Christmas gardens tradition here (Evening Sun 3/5/1957 obit).

'While answering a fire alarm at the home of Paul Costello, 829 Cator avenue, No. 7 truck, of the Waverly Fire Department, stuck in a sewer trap near the scene... released after an hour's work.' Curtains ignited by a gas heater set the Christmas tree ablaze; no insurance.

'Engine Company 31 and Truck Company 7 are at Greenmount and Thirty-second street' (Evening Sun 5/18/1954). Named station personnel from Jeff's clipping set: Capt. Frederick A. Wissing + Lt. John D. LaCon (1947); merit badge to Ira J. Barnes (gas resuscitation, 1950); Capt. William E. Schmidt (1960); Morris Whitehead injured at the Grotz mansion fire, Guilford (1960); Capt. Joseph C. Ruffing, commander, d. 1964 aged 43; James H. Smith assistant engineman (1954); firefighter Cecil K. Lewis assigned 1956 — whose 3-year-old son died in a home fire in 1957. Lost fire hat No. 430, Engine 31, on E 33rd St nr Eastern High (classified, 1947). AFRO 7/9/1960 p17: James H. Duggan of Engine Co. 31 cited for locating an unconscious woman in a smoke-filled house at 3449 Chestnut Ave. CORRECTION to data-room filename: Francis M. Krepner (1956 certificate) was assigned to ENGINE 1, not 31.

Sun 5/30/2010 (Laura Vozzella, 'Renovated Waverly firehouse reopens'): closed June 2009 (pigeons, lead paint, falling windows); first full renovation since the 1970s; Mary Pat Clarke, Capt. John Parker, Chief James S. Clack at the ~100-person reopening. The late-19th-c. Gamewell gong is still part of Engine 31's station alerting system (BCFD Engine 31, 2020). Last wagon in Baltimore's 'Omaha orange' (1990 Sutphen) ran from here 1990-2003.

'No. 4 Chemical Engine Company of Waverly extinguished the flames' — the Bokel store (the 1871 Sun portrait's 'fine brick store... of which Mr. Theodore A. Bokel is proprietor'; initial A.D. vs Theodore A. — likely family succession, initials conflict flagged).

A Maryland Match Co. (Baltimore) matchbook cover: 'GABBY'S CARRY OUT SHOP — PIZZA - SUBS. SPAGHETTI — WE DELIVER — WAVERLY TOWER SHOPPING CENTER, 29th & GREENMOUNT — CH. 3-9158,' with a chef-tossing-Pizza 'Real Italian Style' panel. Physical evidence of the Oriole Park block's retail afterlife: after the 1944 fire cleared the ballpark, the block carried the 'Waverly Tower Shopping Center' — and its pizza carry-out, the corridor's midcentury Italian-American food layer in matchstick form. Dating: two-letter phone exchange + postal zone (no ZIP) place it ~1948-1963; range recorded, artifact undated.

A Maryland Match Co. matchbook cover for 'Hooper's Restaurants': locations 'CHARLES & FAYETTE STS., 3 W. CHESAPEAKE AVE., TOWSON, THE MT. ROYAL HOTEL, 415 E. THIRTY-SECOND STREET, 3130 GREENMOUNT AVENUE — General Offices 415 East 32nd Street, Baltimore 18, Maryland.' The corridor address sits in a chain roster beside the Mt. Royal Hotel and downtown Charles & Fayette — 3130 Greenmount as a white-tablecloth-adjacent chain restaurant location at midcentury. Dating: two-letter phone exchange + postal zone (no ZIP) place it ~1948-1963; range recorded, artifact undated. CONFIRMED: the 1958 Waverly Park & Shop directory lists 'HOOPER'S RESTAURANT, 3130 Greenmount Avenue' (Evening Sun 6/11/1958 p49, img 369952101) — the matchbook location documented in print, mid-chain-roster era.

A Superintendent of Transportation Office photograph (shared by Marvin Welch, Baltimore Past and Present Photos, 10/13/2021): the vast low tabernacle built for evangelist BILLY SUNDAY's 1916 Baltimore campaign, at York Road and 29th Street — 'in the left center background is a sign that reads ORIOLE PARK circa 1915.' Streetcar No. 790 passes on York Road; crowds mill; a horse cart stands at the curb; new rowhouses rise behind. The block's sacred-and-profane double bill: the Federal League ballpark and the sawdust trail side by side. RENUMBERING EVIDENCE in the caption: 'it was situated in 1916 at York Road and 10TH STREET. Only later were these streets renamed Greenmount Avenue and 29th Street' (the cross-streets north of North Ave carried numbers from 9th upward before the 1919-era renumbering; Sun columnist Jacques Kelly, in the thread, disputes how current '10th street' ever was). GEOGRAPHY RESOLVED (agent research: SABR/Wikipedia): the tabernacle stood ACROSS 29th Street from this parcel — on the SOUTHWEST corner block (28th-29th/Greenmount/Barclay), the abandoned AMERICAN LEAGUE PARK site, Waverly's old 'York Road grounds' where professional baseball ran 1889-1914 (Oriole Park II of 1889; the 1901-02 American League Orioles; the International League Orioles through Babe Ruth's 1914 rookie season). The photo thus captures BOTH ballpark blocks at once: the revival shed on the dead park, the 'Oriole Park' sign on the living one (Terrapin, this parcel's block). THE CAMPAIGN (Sun retrospective 7/2/2005 + campaign histories): February 2 - April 23, 1916; the 15,000-seat 'Salvation Shed'; over a million hearers; 23,027 'trail hitters'; ~96,000 through the doors on the final day, when 'Home Run' Baker and four other Yankees hit the sawdust trail. Sunday was himself a former big-league ballplayer — the evangelist-outfielder preaching on a dead ballpark beside a live one.

Declaration of Intention No. 9916, Court of Common Pleas, Baltimore, sworn June 3, 1926: LENA STOLER, aged 36, occupation MERCHANT, 'color white, complexion dark, height 5 feet, weight 98 pounds, hair black, eyes brown,' born HOMEL, RUSSIA (Gomel, today Belarus) March 10, 1890; residing 3208 GREENMOUNT AVENUE; emigrated from 'Lebovg' [Libau/Liepaja] on the vessel NEWLAND, arriving Philadelphia about March 15, 1906, aged ~16; married, husband LOUIS, born Russia, 'now resides with me'; renouncing allegiance 'particularly to THE PRESENT GOVERNMENT OF RUSSIA' — a 1926 formula acknowledging the Soviet state without naming it. A 98-pound merchant-wife running a Greenmount storefront household. STOLER: the same surname as the shoe-store family at 2703 Greenmount (1913-1922, incl. Max Stoler, whose daughter Marian was struck by the York Rd car in 1915) — the family's footprint moving up the avenue; kinship unproven.

A red printed price card: 'RIDGEWOOD COAL COMPANY, BELMONT 8619, 2950 GREENMOUNT AVE. — Stove, No. 3 $17.00 / Nut $17.00 / Pea $16.00 — GUARANTEED COLLIERY COAL, Immediate Delivery.' A coal dealer trading from the 2900 block — the corridor's home-heating economy (the same trade the Phoebus and AALL firms served on the 2600-2700 blocks) in its anthracite generation, sold by stove/nut/pea grades at $16-17 a ton. Dating: the four-digit 'BELMONT 8619' exchange predates the two-letter-five-number format (~1947 cutover) and the prices fit the late-1930s-40s; artifact undated, range recorded.

A color slide of the 3200 block in full cry: the WAVERLY theatre's vertical sign and marquee — 'VINCENT PRICE — TWICE TOLD TALES — TECHNICOLOR' (released July 1963) — with ROBERTS JEWELERS next door, the corner NIFTY CLEANERS ('3 HR shirt service'), Bailey's up the row, a produce stand on the sidewalk, and a yellow PCC car on route 8 loading mid-street among '59-'62 automobiles. The 1909 Forrest-designed picture house still first-run 54 years on — a decade past the existing mid-century listings evidence — and the block's retail ecosystem (jeweler, cleaner, produce) arrayed around it. The streetcar era had months left: route 8 converted to buses in November 1963. AFTERLIFE (agent research, Cinema Treasures/WMS): 692 seats, Durkee-operated; closed as a movie house in 1969 — six years after this frame — and after many conversions the space is SHOE CITY at 3211 Greenmount today: the marquee corner still sells shoes.

'WAITRESSES (2) EXP.—Must know how to wait on tables. Neat-appearing. Sweeney's Cafe, 3128 Greenmount ave.' Sweeney's trading at 3128 by mid-1935 — a post-Repeal cafe-bar hiring floor staff two years into legal liquor.

In the Evening Sun's PROFESSIONAL & AMATEUR classifieds, three weeks after Pearl Harbor: 'AMATEURS WANTED TONIGHT — Cash prizes. Apply 10 P.M. SWEENEY'S CAFE, 3128 Greenmount avenue.' Sweeney's running amateur-night entertainment with cash prizes — the neighborhood cafe as working stage, twenty years before it got its own record.

The Evening Sun's duckpin league schedule, White Division: 'Chris Cafe vs Sweeney's Cafe at Guilford.' The bar in the wartime tavern-league ecosystem — its name bowling alongside Migan's Cafe, C. D. Kenny, Glenn L. Martin and American Beer teams.

In a Sun contribution list, between 'From A Friend $1.00' and 'Thirteen anonymous contributions $97.93': 'PATRONS OF SWEENEY'S CAFE — $63.00.' The regulars pooling a bar-wide gift — the cafe as civic unit, its patrons a named collective in the newspaper.

A 7-inch 45: 'SWEENEY'S TWIST (Billy Martin) — BILLY MARTIN and his Corvairs — MONITOR RECORDS #1402-A, 45 R.P.M., Jalo Music, Inc. - BMI,' b/w 'I Found My Baby' (1962). Per collector documentation (Discogs r4207180; popsike auction notes), the record is a tribute to Sweeney's Lounge on Greenmount Avenue — the bar is named in the lyrics — produced by Baltimore DJ Jack Gale on the local Monitor label. A Greenmount corner bar with its own twist record at the height of the dance craze: place-made IP, pressed in vinyl, still trading among collectors sixty years on (Jeff holds a copy). The through-line from the 1942 amateur nights to the 1962 record is the venue's own: the stage that paid cash prizes eventually paid in canon. PRODUCER IDENTIFIED (agent research 2026-07-15): Jack Gale (1925-2018), Baltimore-born WITH-AM 1230 morning host 1957-63 and later Billboard DJ of the Year (1970), was recording local acts (Ronnie Dove, the Kings, the Combonaires) at Biddle Street Studios in exactly this period; 'JALO' = JAck + LOvey Gale (his wife's public records list The Jalo Corporation and Lovey Music Inc.), and Jalo Records 1406 (Ronnie Dove, June 1962) shares Monitor 1402's numbering series — Monitor was almost certainly a Gale imprint. 'Billy Martin' himself remains unidentified (a Montreal-trumpeter attribution on citizenfreak looks like name-collision; no Baltimore Jam band listing) — possibly a pickup band for the one-off. The side was later anthologized on the 'Buzzsaw Joint Cut 7' compilation LP.

The Waverly Park and Shop directory (Evening Sun, 6/11/1958) lists 'VINSON'S ANIMAL HOSPITAL, 3015 Greenmount Avenue' among the association's 35 members. POSSIBLE family link, unproven: Robert L. and Evelyn D. Vinson bought 2601 Greenmount in May 1961, three years after this listing — a Vinson veterinary practice fifteen blocks up the same avenue. Polk/BLL check queued. UPGRADED (agent research 2026-07-15): Vinson Animal Hospital's own history page says the practice was 'ESTABLISHED IN 1930 OFF OF GREENMOUNT AVE BY DR. VINSON' — at 3015 Greenmount until relocating to Towson in 1993, where it operates today. A Dr. Vinson ran the hospital throughout the very years Robert L. and Evelyn D. Vinson owned 2601 Greenmount (1961-72); the founder's first name is still unconfirmed — Sun obituary of Robert L. Vinson (d. 11/20/1970) is the closing check.

Radio Center's display ad on the Park & Shop page: 'RADIO CENTER IN WAVERLY INVITES YOU TO ENJOY THE BEST IN MUSIC ON RCA CAMDEN — $1.98 YOUR CHOICE, 12 inch L.P. Records' — South Pacific, Perry Como's Dream Along With Me, Boston Pops 1812 Overture, and a forty-title Camden catalog printed in full; 'RADIO CENTER, 3118 GREENMOUNT AVE., BE. 5-6898, Appliance Sales and Service.' The avenue's record store, two doors from Sweeney's Cafe — the retail end of the Greenmount sound stratum (Sweeney's stage 1942, its 45 in 1962, the National Recording Studio at 3016 by the 1980s).

The Park & Shop directory lists 'WHITE COFFEE POT, 3200 Greenmount Avenue' — the Waverly location of the Baltimore 24-hour chain whose matchbook ('Good Meals at Sensible Prices — Restaurants All Around Baltimore — OPEN 24 HOURS,' Jeff's collection, Round 5f) previously lacked an address. The corner of 32nd: coffee around the clock beside Read's Drug and the new parking lot.

The Sun, 5/5/2021 (Tkacik): Red Emma's — 'Baltimore's cooperatively-run, radical bookstore and cafe' — announced the purchase of TWO buildings for its forever home: 415 E. 32nd Street and THIS storefront at 3128 Greenmount Avenue, with support from state Neighborhood Business Initiative grants, the Central Baltimore Partnership, Central Baltimore Future Fund and Waverly Main Street. The venue lineage of 3128 runs unbroken: Sweeney's Cafe's amateur nights with cash prizes (1942), the bar immortalized on 'Sweeney's Twist' (Monitor #1402, 1962), and now a worker-owned bookstore-cafe whose readings, shows and organizing meetings put a stage back in the room. The 1958 Park & Shop association's descendant — Waverly Main Street — helped land it: the district's coordinated-retail muscle, 63 years on, recruiting its anchor. THE TRANSACTION (agent research, SDAT open data + liquor board, 2026-07-15): the deal closed January 12, 2022 — $800,000 for BOTH parcels in one arms-length multi-parcel transfer from 415 EAST 32ND STREET, LLC (deeds Liber 18420/348 for 3128 Greenmount; Liber 18262/191 for 415 E 32nd). The seller LLC had assembled the pair in 2016: 3128 bought 8/31/2016 for $376,500 from J.T.M. Greenmount, LLC, and 415 E 32nd bought 7/1/2016 for $240,000 from THOMAS R. FANNIN — Early Attic's proprietor owned his building. Financing: Seed Commons committed a $1 million non-extractive renovation line/mortgage (mortgage payment ~half the co-op's prior rent). The entity: RED EMMA'S COOPERATIVE CORPORATION (Baltimore liquor board, July 2022 — a Class B license requesting LIVE ENTERTAINMENT, principals Mary Al-Khatib and Andrew Scotti). Soft opening at 3128: late October 2022. The live-entertainment license makes the venue lineage official.

The Sun's twist-era retrospective ('Twistin' the night away,' 7/30/1991) ranks the room first: 'Sweeney's on Greenmount Avenue may have been the most popular, but there were many others' — ahead of the Surf Club, the Celebrity Lounge, Cicero's (where Ronnie Dove's Original Twisters played) and Gussie's Downbeat. Baltimore Brew (5/3/2021, on Red Emma's arrival): 'Old-timers may remember 3128 Greenmount as the home of Sweeney's Cocktail Lounge, which advertised three multi-level bars, a dance-a-rama for happy fun loving patrons and, for its grand opening, offered a cash prize to the lady with the most beautiful bonnet.' The Better Waverly walking-tour brochure (2010) files it in the neighborhood's legendary bar constellation ('...Green Door, Northside, Judge's, Sweeney's, Schuman's, Donohue's, Dutchman's...'), and baltimorejam.org lists Sweeney's Lounge among 1960s live-music venues. A 1940s Sweeney's Cafe matchbook survives in the collector market. Proprietor identity still unfound — Polk/liquor-notice thread open.

The 2016 deed's metes-and-bounds (Exhibit A of Liber 18420/348) measure 3128 Greenmount Avenue from 'the southwest corner of Greenmount Avenue (formerly YORK TURNPIKE ROAD) and MERRYMAN'S LANE' (now East 33rd Street) and recite that the ground was 'heretofore leased by AUSTIN DALL, TRUSTEE, to MARY ANN LYTTLE, by Lease recorded in Baltimore COUNTY in Liber J.B. No. 107, folio 578.' That is a pre-annexation record — this stretch of the York Road was Baltimore County until the 1888 city extension — making the Dall-to-Lyttle lease the oldest instrument yet cited anywhere on the 3100 block of Greenmount. Merryman's Lane (33rd Street) ties directly to the corridor's original land grants (Merryman's Lot, 1688). The parcel is 25 x 200 feet, 65 feet south of the 33rd-Street corner.

The 2016 deed's Exhibit A 'saves and excepts' a piece at the rear of 3128 — 'all that piece or parcel of ground granted and conveyed by the Boulevard Realty, Inc. unto Dashiell by Deed dated April 6, 1938 and recorded ... in Liber MLP No. 5812, folio 312, with the right in the grantee to the use of the party wall.' This is the same Ella V. W. Dashiell / Boulevard Realty developer pair that built and subdivided the 415-421 East 32nd Street row one block south (see 415 E 32nd). The 1938 conveyance carved the 32nd-Street/Brentwood-Avenue building lots out of the older Greenmount frontage — the moment the deep corner lot was split between its Greenmount face (3128) and its 32nd-Street rear (415-421).

The immediate predecessor in title: by deed dated February 7, 2007 (Liber FMC 9054, folio 112) '3128 Greenmount Avenue, LLC' conveyed the tract to 'J.T.M. Greenmount, LLC,' the Anthony Farnella entity that held the corner until the 2016 sale to Red Emma's holding company. Recited in the 2016 deed as the source of J.T.M.'s title.

Deed dated August 19, 2016 (Liber 18420, folio 348): J.T.M. Greenmount, LLC (Anthony Farnella, Managing Member) grants 3128 Greenmount Avenue — plus the Brentwood-Avenue gore behind it — in FEE SIMPLE to 415 East 32nd Street, LLC, the holding entity of the RED EMMA'S BOOKSTORE COFFEEHOUSE worker cooperative, for $376,500. Prepared by Henry I. Louis, attorney (1615 York Road, Lutherville); notarized in Howard County by Karen Ann Wirtz. Paired with the same-day $240,000 leasehold assignment of 415-421 East 32nd Street (Liber 18262/191), it completes Red Emma's assemblage of the corner — $616,500 total — the co-op's purchase of a permanent home after years of moving. The deed's own metes-and-bounds carry the parcel's history back through the 2007 J.T.M. deed, the 1938 Boulevard/Dashiell split, and the pre-annexation Dall-to-Lyttle Baltimore County ground lease.

In November 1843 the Rev. W. A. Hewitt was sent to the village of Huntingdon by the Rt. Rev. William Rollinson Whittingham, Bishop of Maryland, at the request of Mr. THOMAS HART, who wished to have his grandchildren baptized without the journey to the mother parish, St. Paul's, downtown. The congregation was born with those baptisms and the ideals of the OXFORD (Tractarian) MOVEMENT that Bishop Whittingham was planting in Maryland. Huntingdon was then a village of some seventeen great estates (Montebello, Clover Hill, Homewood, Guilford, Greenmount, Homestead); it was annexed to Baltimore City in 1888 and renamed Waverly after Scott's novels. On 24 November 1843 Bishop Whittingham himself preached in the congregation's temporary chapel. St. John's is the anchor of a three-parcel campus that survives today: the church and its 1.83-acre churchyard (3009½ Greenmount), the rectory (3001 Old York Road), and this 1914 parish hall (3009 Greenmount).

The congregation's first services were held in an old REVOLUTIONARY WAR BARRACKS standing about thirty yards southwest of the present church. On 10 July 1844 St. John's was legally incorporated as a diocesan mission church within the bounds of St. Paul's parish; by 1845 it was an independent congregation.

The cornerstone of the first church was laid 22 April 1846; it was consecrated by Bishop Whittingham on 11 November 1847, and it was resolved that St. John's would be a 'FREE' CHURCH — NO PEW RENTS, ever, an egalitarian stance for the era. For two years the rector returned his stipend toward the building and installed the furnace at his own expense. The 1847 building (which stood on the church parcel, 3009½ Greenmount) is attributed by the CHAP Landmark Report to ROBERT CARY LONG JR. (1810-1849), Baltimore's leading Gothic Revival architect — an attribution absent from the parish's own history and from the 1975 National Register form (which assigns no architect and names Abraham Bucher as 'in charge of building').

In 1866 the parish built a stone Gothic Revival schoolhouse on this lot — $6,000, funded by Mrs. HANNAH D. WYMAN — in matching 'gothick' style. The Wyman family were St. John's principal benefactors (Samuel Wyman funded the bell tower and slate roof; Hannah the school). This schoolhouse stood where the 1914 parish hall now stands; the poet Lizette Woodworth Reese taught in the parish school.

The 1866 stone schoolhouse was replaced in 1914 by the present PARISH HALL at 3009 Greenmount (this parcel), designed by architect NORMAN E. HORN, built of Falls Road granite by A. E. Schoenlein & Son for $25,000. This is the building the Diocese of Maryland began renovating in 2023 into classrooms and a commercial kitchen — and the only one of the three campus parcels deeded out of the parish (to the BIT Community Center in 2024).

In June 2016 the Rev. Jesse L. A. Parker — twelfth rector, who from 1994 led the interior restoration with decorative artist Janet Pope of J. Pope Studios — retired after 25 years. That September the Rev. JEFFREY CHARLES HUAL ('Father Jeff') became Priest-in-Charge, from a curacy at St. Paul's Parish, K Street, Washington, D.C. Earlier rectors of record: W. A. Hewitt (first, 1843/45); the Rev. Thomas Richey, D.D. (rector in 1879, later a General Theological Seminary professor); and R. Douglas Pitt (eleventh, who began the restoration 1983-85).

In October 2017 the Diocese of Maryland formally declared St. John's an 'imperiled parish.' Membership, 143 in 2015, would fall to 72 by 2023 as the congregation worked through the imperilment seeking financial stability.

The Diocesan Council approved 'the closing of St John's in the Village, Baltimore, effective April 10, 2023, having been imperiled and struggling for several years' (2023 Diocesan Convention Journal, Part A); management of the campus transferred to the Diocese effective 17 April 2023. Membership at closure was 72 (from 143 in 2015); the 2024 parochial report shows zero members, zero pledge income, zero average attendance. The last bishop's visitation had been 18 September 2022. After 180 years, the free church of the village of Huntingdon held its last service.

Rather than sell or deconsecrate the campus, the Diocese of Maryland repurposed it. Per the Baltimore Sun (22 Nov 2023) the diocese would renovate this 1914 parish hall into classrooms and a commercial kitchen for the SUTTON SCHOLARS high-school mentorship program and the BIT COMMUNITY CENTER, INC. (formerly the Italian Cultural Center of Maryland / 'B-More Pasta,' founder Monica Lapenta). The chain: St. John's Church Vestry → Diocese of Maryland (deed 26946/26, 2023) → BIT Community Center, Inc. (deed 27169/1, conveyed for no consideration, recorded 29 Aug 2024). Only this parcel was deeded out; the church-with-cemetery and the rectory remain titled to the Vestry. [Upgrades the prior SDAT-stub incident.]

In 1850 the lot in the rear was purchased for the CEMETERY, with the first burial that same year (in 1849 the south lot had been bought from Dr. W. T. Wilson for the parish school, in 1854 a lot for the parsonage). The churchyard — about 1.83 acres, on this parcel (3009½ Greenmount) behind the church — grew to hold nearly 600 graves (Find A Grave cemetery #2219356). Its earliest stones (Malvina J. Ross, d.1820; Mary Hall Chew, d.1837) predate the 1850 lot and mark re-interments from the founding families.

Eleven years after its consecration, the first St. John's church was destroyed by fire. A contemporary account in The Daily Exchange (Baltimore), May 17, 1858 — 'Incendiarism. Burning of a Church in the County' — reports the fire discovered between 1 and 2 a.m. on May 16, 1858 (RESOLVING the CHAP-vs-parish-history date discrepancy in favor of May 16), destroying the church built ~1848 in 'plain Gothic style, of dark granite'; only the walls stood. Insured for just $1,700, 'far from covering the loss.' Rev. George F. Adams was pastor. 'The impression prevails that the church was first robbed of all valuables therein, and then fired' — matching the CHAP report's arson finding. The blaze lit up the sky as far as the city; most Baltimore fire companies halted at Green Mount Cemetery, too distant to help, and only the Independent Company reached the scene, too late to save the building. The Vestry's $200 reward went unclaimed; the arsonists were never caught.

The cornerstone of the present church was laid on the old foundations by Bishop Whittingham on 11 September 1858; first service 22 May 1859; consecrated All Saints' Day, 1 November 1860 (Samuel Wyman gave $2,000 toward the debt). Designed by New York architect JOHN WELLER PRIEST (1825-1859) — a founding member of the American Institute of Architects and the American architect recommended by the Ecclesiological Society — it was patterned after ST. MICHAEL'S, LONG STANTON, England: pure English 'country gothick' of long nave, lancet windows, thick low medieval walls and steep roof. As first built it was only the first four nave bays with a south porch and a new tower. Scharf's 1881 history records St. John's as a MOTHER CHURCH: the mission that became St. Michael's & All Angels' 'was originally a mission of St. John's Church, Waverly.'

In 1875 the church was enlarged into its cruciform shape: transepts, a baptistery (now the Lady Chapel), a sacristy, an enlarged sanctuary, and the bell tower and spire. Designed by HENRY MARTYN CONGDON (1834-1922) of New York — Priest's protege, an AIA Fellow — who also designed the reredos; builder W. H. Allen of Baltimore; Samuel Wyman paid for the new slate roof. (The 1975 National Register form dates this campaign 1878 and credits an 1849 tower plan to Frank Wills.) Interior decoration was completed in 1895; the original decoration was restored 1983-85 (Rev. R. Douglas Pitt) and from 1994 by decorative artist Janet Pope, J. Pope Studios. The stained glass makers, organ builder and bell founder remain undocumented online.

In September 1885 a boys' orphanage opened in a frame house on the northeast portion of the church property (the late Rev. Johnston had given toward it; in 1875 Richard C. Hull donated a parcel for a charitable institution). The orphanage closed around 1912 and its building was later sold as a private residence.

St. John's ~1.83-acre churchyard (Find A Grave #2219356, ~583 memorials, earliest death 1820) holds a remarkable roster. DR. RICHARD WILMOT HALL (1785-1847) — twice DEAN of the University of Maryland School of Medicine, professor of obstetrics, a War of 1812 surgeon and author of 'Memoirs of Military Surgery' — lies here; his and his wife Eliza Taylor Hall's portraits hang in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. THOMAS ROBERT HART (1788-1850), whose request for his grandchildren's baptism founded the parish, is buried in the churchyard he created. The Maryland State Archives' Civil War Burials survey (SC6197) indexes SEVEN Civil War veterans here — six Confederate, including Lt. David Stone Briscoe of MOSBY'S RANGERS (43rd Va. Cavalry), Lt. Col. William F. Beasley, surgeon Dr. Arthur Brogden, Adjt. Robertson Taylor, Pvt. Charles W. Daniell; one Union soldier, Pvt. John H. Cooper (51st N.Y.); and Sister Margaret Hickey, a Church Home Hospital nurse who 'cared for both northern and southern troops.' Founding families (Hart, Hall, Chew, Gabler, Baldwin, Aitken, Ellicott) recur across the stones.

In 1937 twenty Scotch and Austrian pines and a white English hawthorn were planted in the churchyard in memory of LIZETTE WOODWORTH REESE (1856-1935), one of Baltimore's most celebrated poets — memoirist of 'A Victorian Village' and 'The Old House in the Country' — who had taught in the St. John's parish school and is INTERRED in this churchyard. An unmarked section at the rear holds servant burials.

St. John's Protestant Episcopal Church was individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 27 March 1974 (reference #74002214; Maryland Historical Trust file NR-212, survey B-3731). It was later designated a Baltimore City Landmark by the Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation on 8 April 2014.

St. John's tower bells (from the 1875 campaign) rang the hours 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. and, in 1994-97, drew a documented neighborhood noise dispute covered by the Baltimore Sun (26 Feb 1997), with the Rev. Jesse L. A. Parker as rector — a small human-scale episode in the parish's late history.

The St. John's Rectory at 3001 Old York Road was built in 1868 (the parsonage lot had been purchased in 1854), congregation-funded in matching 'gothick' style; its architect is unknown (the CHAP report suggests a pattern book; the city assessment dates the structure 1872). It served as the parish's clergy residence and remains the parish's mailing address. One of the three surviving parcels of the St. John's campus (with the church + churchyard at 3009½ Greenmount and the 1914 parish hall at 3009 Greenmount); after the 2023 closure it remains titled to the St. John's Church Vestry, held for the Diocese of Maryland.

The CHAP Landmark Report (Apr 8, 2014, p. 6) records, in one sentence: 'While most burials have a marker (and there are hundreds), there is an unmarked section in the rear of the church where the servants were buried.' That is the ONLY institutional acknowledgment of these dead — and its lone source, endnote 39, is 'Father Jesse Parker, personal communication, March 29, 2014': a single oral statement from the rector, resting on no burial register, plat, or survey. The published record is silent on everything more specific — whether the servants were enslaved or free, their race, their number, their dates, or whose households they served. What CAN be documented is the surrounding world: the cemetery's rear lot opened in 1850; Maryland held people in slavery until Nov 1, 1864, and (per the diocese's own 2007 history, Klein & Smith, 'Racism in the Anglican and Episcopal Church of Maryland') its Episcopal parishes were 'almost entirely segregated' — so a section set apart from the marked family plots is fully consistent with the pattern (enslaved people before 1864, free Black and immigrant domestics after). The parish's leading benefactor, Samuel Wyman, bought the Homewood estate in 1839; Homewood is the corridor's most-documented slavery site — but its documented enslaved history (Johns Hopkins' 'Enslaved at Homewood') is the CARROLL era through 1836, BEFORE Wyman, and Wyman-era slaveholding is not established by available sources. The poet Lizette Woodworth Reese, buried in this same churchyard, portrayed Waverly's Black domestic community in her memoir 'A Victorian Village' (1929) — 'Daddy Black and Others,' 'old black Eli... the butler' — but did not tie them to these graves. The Episcopal Diocese of Maryland's 'Trail of Souls' slavery-reckoning project (2014; a ~$1.39M reparations fund) invites every parish founded before 1864 to research its ties to slavery; St. John's qualifies (founded 1843) but has NOT participated — it is absent from the project and the diocesan history. So these servants remain, for now, real stakeholders in this ground whose story has not been told: the honest next step is the primary research St. John's has not done — burial registers, vestry minutes, and a physical survey of the rear section — that would let them be counted and, where possible, named.

Robertson Taylor (1840–1924), coffee-and-sugar importer of the clipper-ship era who organized the firm Taylor & Levering and was later with the U.S. Fidelity & Guaranty Co. A native of Norfolk, Va., he came to Baltimore in 1865 just after Appomattox, having served throughout the Civil War in the Confederate Army — enlisting as a private, promoted (per the obituary) to colonel, and wounded at the Battle of the Wilderness. He helped organize and establish the Protestant Episcopal Church of St. Michael and All Angels (the parish St. John's, Waverly, had spawned), and donated the houses at Charles and Twentieth Streets that became a hospital for crippled children — later the Kernan Hospital and Industrial School. Died Oct. 15, 1924 at his summer home in Carroll County, age 84; interred in St. John's churchyard (Find A Grave #30939895). Note: his Find A Grave record lists him as Adjutant, 6th Virginia Infantry — a rank discrepancy with the obituary's 'colonel.'

Oliver Perry Baldwin (d. July 17, 1878), of the editorial staff of The Baltimore Sun (earlier a Richmond newspaper editor). On July 29, 1878 the Sun ran a front-page memorial tribute written — anonymously, at his own wish — by Professor George Frederick Holmes of the University of Virginia, opening with Hamlet's line for Yorick ('Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio; a fellow of infinite jest') and praising his wit, learning, and 'unstinted generosity which embraced all conditions.' Interred in St. John's churchyard, Waverly (Find A Grave #32287331).

Nathaniel Chew (c.1834–1905), of the Chew family, early Huntingdon/Waverly gentry. Son of Washington P. and Mary Hall Chew of Havre de Grace (a Chew–Hall marriage tie; his mother shares the name of the Mary Hall Chew, d.1837, among the churchyard's earliest stones). Brother of James W. Chew, longtime clerk of the U.S. District Court. He lived in retirement at 1431 Madison Avenue, where he died Nov. 14, 1905 at age 71; his funeral was held from St. John's Protestant Episcopal Church, Waverly (Find A Grave #32289322).

James White Chew (d. Jan. 9, 1907), for more than 50 years Clerk of the United States Circuit Court and District Courts of Baltimore. Brother of Nathaniel Chew; the two shared the family home at 1431 Madison Avenue, where he died of Bright's disease. His funeral was held from St. George's Protestant Episcopal Church (Pressman and Division Streets), conducted by Rev. Thomas Atkinson, rector of St. Barnabas', with burial in St. John's churchyard, Waverly (Find A Grave #32289346).

New York Times obituary (June 21, 1932): Oliver Perry Baldwin Jr., ~50 years on the editorial staff of The Baltimore Sun and its managing editor during the 1904 Baltimore fire, died at his Baltimore home June 20, 1932, aged 82. Born Richmond 1850, son of Sun editor O.P. Baldwin; UVA law, Maryland legislator, late-life anti-Prohibition leader. Survived by widow Caroline Frances Sutton, daughters Anna Lee and Dorothy, and son Hanson W. Baldwin of The New York Times (later Pulitzer-winning military editor). Buried St. John's, Waverly.

The Maryland General Assembly passed 'An act to divorce Elizabeth Blakeley, and her husband John Blakeley, of Baltimore county' (reported passing in the Maryland Gazette, Annapolis, Jan. 25, 1827) — a legislative divorce, decades before Maryland's courts could grant one. This John Blakeley appears to be the one buried at St. John's (1803-1860): he would have been about 24 in 1827, and his churchyard wife Maria Elizabeth Robinson (b.1820) was far too young to be the 'Elizabeth' of the act — consistent with Elizabeth being a divorced first wife and Maria a later marriage. Identification is a strong lead, not yet confirmed against the session-law text (Laws of Maryland, Dec. 1826 session) or Meyer's 'Divorces and Names Changed in Maryland by Act of the Legislature, 1634-1867'.
