Charles B. Baker bought the old City school property at Greenmount Avenue & 33rd Street at public auction for $75,400, subject to an irredeemable $50 ground rent — the origin of what became the 'Baker Block.' The lot fronted 193 feet on 33rd St and 143 feet on Greenmount and held a schoolhouse of the first school district; contents (books, desks, furniture) had been removed before the sale. The city had tried the previous winter to sell the site to the American Oil Company for $48,700 for a drive-in filling station, but the City Council refused to ratify that deal after opposition (there were already filling stations at the SW and NE corners of Greenmount & 33rd). Reoffered at auction (Meyers & Meyers, auctioneers), bidding opened with New York's Morris Schapiro at $70,000, climbed past a Board of Estimates-appraised value of $47,500, and came down to a final duel between Schapiro ($75,350) and Baker, who topped him at $75,400. Other bidders included Lester L. Smith ($45,500), Thomas J. McDonald ($37,000) and William A. Harris ($50,000); American Oil's Louis Blaustein — the company's founder — had made an unsuccessful individual offer of $50,000 to the Board of Estimates before the auction. The sale proceeds were earmarked to help pay off the mortgage the city took to buy the Hoen Building (A. Hoen & Co.'s former lithography plant) as a City Hall annex under the Broening administration — directly tying the Baker Block's origin to the corridor's other marquee 19th-century name, August Hoen.

Nov 1, 1924: the Mayor and City Council formally conveyed title to the school property (southwest corner of 33rd & Greenmount) to C. B. Baker, about a month after the Sept 1924 auction. Baker immediately reconveyed a 40x95 ft portion at the southeast corner of Talbott & 33rd Streets to George M. Doebereiner — a confectioner who ran a business on the 33rd St side of the emerging block — for $20,000, through the Maryland Title Guarantee Company, calling it an investment.

Jul 29, 1926: construction announced for the Baker Block — 'Business Structure To Rise On Site Of Old School At Waverly.' A one-story-and-basement stucco building, architects Smith & May, ~140 ft frontage on Greenmount Ave and ~150 ft on 33rd St, containing EIGHT stores on Greenmount and FOUR on 33rd Street; the $100,000 contract was to be awarded that day, with completion expected by late October 1926. This CORRECTS the National Register/CHAP dating of the Baker Block to 'ca. 1925' — construction was actually contracted and built in 1926. Lee E. Hartman & Co. were the leasing agents for the property (the same firm that brokered Woolworth's 1927 lease here).

Jul 31, 1926: the construction contract for the Baker Block (SW corner of 33rd & Greenmount, on the recently-demolished school site) was awarded to Thomas Hicks & Sons, builders, for the ~$100,000 stucco commercial building.

May 6, 1927: F. W. Woolworth Company signed a 20-year lease for the storefront building at 3228-3230 Greenmount Avenue, near 33rd St, from C. B. Baker — one of three long-term leases the chain closed that day (also 2102-4-6 E. Monument St and a Westminster, Md. store), all through broker Lee E. Hartman & Co. This confirms the exact Woolworth address within the Baker Block.

Feb 1928: C. B. Baker leased the stores at 423 and 425 East Thirty-third Street to W. H. Wiley for automobile-showroom purposes, for two years with a three-year option, through brokers F. N. Iglehart & Co. — likely two of the four 33rd St-facing storefronts in the newly-built Baker Block (which had ~150 ft of 33rd St frontage), though canon does not yet have separate Property rows for these two addresses, so this is pinned to the Baker Block anchor parcel pending that split.

Mitchell Courthouse to foreclose on QT HAU, LLC's Dec 10, 2021 Purchase Money Deed of Trust (Liber 24654, Folio 362) covering the whole combined tax lot -- Tax ID 12-20-3882-012, described by the auction house as '3226-3240 Greenmount Ave., includes 419-427 E. 33rd St.,' ~22,910 sq ft (0.526 ac), ~19,000 sq ft of retail building in 8 rental units. City of Baltimore Department of Public Works property plat of Block 3882 (Ward 12, Section 20; scale 1in=50ft; dated May 1930) shows lots 12 and 13 already combined into one parcel ("12/13") fronting Greenmount Ave between Merryman Lane and E 33rd St -- the Baker Block footprint -- alongside the triangular lot arrangement along Merryman Lane/Brentwood Ave to the north. Confirms the combined 12/13 lot (now assessed as lot 012) is not a modern artifact of a later consolidation but was already unified by 1930, within a few years of the Baker Block's 1926 construction. May 14, 1976: '13-7, Inc.' filed a UCC-1 financing statement with First Maryland Leasecorp for a full restaurant equipment package at 3236 Greenmount Ave -- Custom Keating electric griddle, three-section roll warmer, refrigerated worktable, Scotsman ice flaker, six-foot compartment sink, Jet Spray drink dispenser, stainless steel worktables/hand sinks, Plexiglass display sign and menu board, coffeemaker, exhaust hood/duct/fan, table and chairs. Confirms a diner/restaurant operator ('13-7, Inc.') at 3236 Greenmount -- a middle storefront in the Baker Block strip -- continuing the corner's long restaurant-succession pattern (Hasslinger 1927-28, Boulevard/Anderson family 1945, Godfrey's Steer and Beer 1970). June 3, 1935: Charles B. Baker, by then 'of Shadwell, Albemarle County, Virginia, formerly of Baltimore County,' executed a Declaration of Trust (recorded amongst the Land Records of Baltimore City in Liber M.L.P. No. 6102, folio 614, 'as well as elsewhere') declaring that he held certain property -- including the Waverly/Greenmount & 33rd corner he'd bought at the 1924 city auction -- as Trustee for the benefit of members of his family. This resolves the apparent 61-year title-chain gap between the 1924 purchase and the 1985 sale to Greenmount Avenue LP: no intervening SALE ever occurred because Baker simply declared his own existing property held in trust for his family -- a self-declaration requires no new deed. Directly corroborated in Baker's own words by a Dec 15, 1949 resignation instrument (Liber M.L.P. No. 7962, folio 5) he personally signed -- see PropertyIncident for that instrument. The 'as well as elsewhere' phrase suggests the 1935 declaration was recorded across more than one jurisdiction (Baker was a Virginia resident by then), which is likely why the Baltimore City folio 614 citation, jumped to directly, showed an unrelated 1940 mortgage instrument rather than the trust text -- probably a cross-reference stub rather than the full declaration.

Feb 22, 1983 (recorded Jun 24, 1983; Book 70, pp. 800-806): Robert M. Goldman, Charles B. Baker Jr., and The First National Bank of Maryland -- Substituted Trustees of 'the Trust U/D of Charles B. Baker' (the 1935 self-declared family trust) -- conveyed the Waverly corner out of the trust to Charles B. Baker Jr. and Rachel Anne Fleet jointly. The deed recites the trust's succession history: Fred Metzger had renounced serving as Substituted Co-Trustee by notices dated Mar 19, 1951 and Jul 8, 1955 (Liber M.L.P. 8394 folio 18 and M.L.P. 10120 folio 172), after which Charles B. Baker Jr. was appointed Substituted Co-Trustee, and Carrie S. Baker (the elder Baker's widow) was appointed Co-Trustee upon and after Charles B. Baker's death. This 1983 distribution -- splitting the property between Baker Jr. and Rachel Anne Fleet -- directly explains why the Dec 1985 deed to Greenmount Avenue LP (PropertyIncident #18788) conveyed only a ONE-HALF interest for $312,500: Baker Jr. held exactly half, with Fleet (presumably a sibling) holding the other half via a probably-companion deed not yet located.

Dec 15, 1949 (recorded Jan 4, 1950; Liber M.L.P. No. 7962, folio 5): Charles B. Baker, in his own hand and words ('of Shadwell, Albemarle County, Virginia, and formerly of Baltimore County, State of Maryland'), resigned as Trustee of the 1935 family trust and appointed the First National Bank of Baltimore and Raphael Walter of Baltimore City as successor trustees -- exercising a right he'd reserved under paragraph 9 of the original 1935 Declaration of Trust. This is the first of two successor-trustee appointments recited in the 1983 distribution deed (PropertyIncident, source mdlandrec/mdlandrec-baker-trust-1983-distribution): Fred Metzger (who must have succeeded Raphael Walter or First National Bank at some point) later renounced serving as Substituted Co-Trustee in 1951 and 1955, after which Charles B. Baker Jr. was appointed in his place.

William T. Datcher, 18, of 3205 Barclay St, drowned in the Jones Falls below the old Cedar Avenue bridge (the Timanus dam; the site is now Round Falls, under Wyman Park Drive) on July 16, 1930. On the 1937 HOLC Residential Security Map, the Oriole Park (V) ground at 30th & Greenmount lies within the ONLY place in Baltimore where all four grades converge: C (yellow, the ballpark block), D (red, across Greenmount into Better Waverly and in the Abell wedge), B (blue, ~four blocks west toward Charles/Guilford), and A (green, north in Oakenshawe). Insight first named by Dr. Lawrence Brown (2026-07-23). VERIFIED 2026-07-24 by computation against the full national Mapping Inequality polygon set (10,154 areas / 314 surveys / 197 all-four-grade cities): Baltimore has a single connected four-grade convergence region citywide (convergence radius R*=81m, ~one block) — so "the only such place in Baltimore" is TRUE. The tightest junction is actually two triple-points ~200m apart (A-B-D and A-C-D). Measured from the ballpark's 30th St edge: the southern junction (A-C-D, on Greenmount just above E 32nd) is ~340 m - about 2.5 blocks - due north; the 81 m ring's center ~3.5 blocks. The ballpark parcel sits INSIDE zone C4, with the D6 wedge passing ~101 m east of it. NOTE: the national-rarity claim is NOT supported — Baltimore ranks 37/197 (five cities have a mathematically perfect single-point four-corners Baltimore lacks). The Federal Home Loan Bank Board, through HOLC, launched the Waverly Community Conservation Test — a WPA field survey (Mar 15–Aug 15, 1939) using a 132-item schedule and at least two photographs of each of the 1,629 buildings in the 39-block, ~163-acre Waverly area (33rd to 42nd Streets, Greenmount Avenue to Ellerslie Avenue/Argonne Drive). The Baltimore Housing Authority sponsored it; the U.S. Housing Authority and HOLC supplied technical services.

The FHLBB published *Waverly: A Study in Neighborhood Conservation* (1940), prepared by economist Arthur Goodwillie under HOLC Deputy General Manager Donald H. McNeal, making the Waverly neighborhood the federal government's national demonstration project for 'neighborhood conservation' — the preventive alternative to slum demolition and a direct ancestor of postwar urban renewal. The 107-page book was offered 'for the inspiration and guidance of other urban communities... throughout the United States.' Waverly was chosen as the 'almost ideal' setting for 'an experimental study in scientific neighborhood conservation.'

The 1940 study defined 'Waverly' as the white residential area north of 33rd Street; it described the district to its south — which includes the Oriole Park (V) ground at 29th–30th & Greenmount — as 'a fully developed... slum district' where 'occupancy is being gradually relinquished to an economically needy and racially mixed residential type,' and which was 'definitely threatening the Area — by its contiguity and by actual infiltration.' The two were separated only by 'a wedge-shaped tract, improved with modern homes... narrow at the west and continuously widening toward the east,' and 'the slum's pressure to cross this sharply defined barrier... [had] been successfully resisted hitherto only by means of the high neighborhood standards.'

The report's summary Table No. 24, 'Dominant Factors in Waverly,' listed under Social conditions the very first factor — 'Race' — with the Favorable entry 'All white.' The study coded its central danger as 'the infiltration of families having more limited earning capacity and lower living and civic standards than their own,' and its Drawing No. 4 mapped 'areas of white and colored occupancy.' A 'well-maintained Negro settlement' of Morgan College teaching staff on Arlington Avenue, land held by 'a group of Negro bankers,' and St. Elizabeth's Home for Female Colored Orphans are named among the Area's environs.

The study documented the federal mortgage apparatus at work in Waverly: the Federal Housing Administration had graded the neighborhood from 58 ('eligible but poor') to 84 ('good') for mortgage-insurance eligibility, refusing Title II insurance anywhere rated below 50; and the Home Owners' Loan Corporation held 122 mortgages and owned 20 properties in the Area — 'the largest single property holder in the Area.'

To make the conservation program permanent, the study established the Waverly Conservation League, incorporated June 13, 1940, with organizing personnel supplied by HOLC: an Advisory Committee of 25 (including the executive heads of the four local improvement associations), an Operating Committee with a chairman from each of the Area's six districts, and 'block captains' for each block. It prescribed 'beneficial restrictions' — deed covenants limiting land to single-family residential use, which it framed as 'effective protection against undesirable infiltration' — and proposed a municipal Department of Conservation to run 'clean-up, paint-up, fix-up' campaigns and enforce restrictions.

The study's Appendix C proposed model legislation drawn from the Waverly experiment — a 'Neighborhood Improvement Act' and an 'Urban Redevelopment Corporations Act' — as templates for other jurisdictions, and the FHLBB explicitly offered the whole formula for 'the treatment of similarly threatened small-home neighborhoods everywhere... increasingly great urban districts throughout the United States.' The Waverly Test thus fed the legal and administrative machinery that became postwar urban renewal.

Before the corridor was built up, Charles Hamilton kept hothouses and flower gardens on York Road 'a little below the tollgate' (Gilmore Lane & York Road = today's Vineyard Lane & Greenmount Ave). He ran gardener want-ads through the 1870s, opened the Waverly Hotel in 1870, held the county contract to supply the courthouse park with flowers, and by 1890 his daughter Ella ran for Waverly postmistress — a horticultural village on the ground the ballpark and stores would later cover.

Polk's 1903 directory listed 'Colored School No. 115' at Merryman Lane near York Road (branch at Barclay near Merryman Lane) and the white 'School No. 51' separately nearby — segregated public education mapped block by block a short walk from the ballground, three decades before the 1937 HOLC map drew the same lines in color.

When the city extended its limits and renamed the old York Road 'Greenmount Avenue,' Waverly residents fought it, arguing the name was coined 'to boom the Greenmount Cemetery' and fearing 'the York road will be unknown.' The spine of the whole wedge had its very name contested — erasure by relabeling.

A Sun kitchen-column recipe submitted by Mrs. J. Merryman of 608 Homestead St., Waverly (blocks from the ballpark): a marble cake with a 'White Portion' (egg whites, white sugar) and a 'Dark Portion' (yolks, molasses, brown sugar), 'each part in turn in a cake pan' — two batters marbled in one tin but never blended, signed with the surname of the 1688 co-grantees of the wedge, a documented Baltimore County enslaving family. (Surname resonance; direct descent not established — the power is the echo.)

When Terrapin Park opened, the city met it with force: 75 officers under Capt. Moxley at the park, 50 more at Oriole Park across the corner, a uniformed man 'at practically every corner' out the York Road, and a mounted squad. Traffic was scripted — 'all vehicles must enter Twenty-ninth street from the York road and go on through to Guilford avenue.' From day one the wedge was a place the police surrounded, choreographed, and controlled.

Before the pennant and the fire, a vast wooden revival tabernacle for evangelist Billy Sunday stood at the wedge — York Road & 29th, the exact corner — drawing crowds past the streetcar barns, an 'Oriole Park' sign already visible in the background. Mass religion and mass transit on the same corner the ballpark, the boycott, and the fire would each claim in turn. The photo also confirms the York Rd→Greenmount / 10th→29th renaming.

A decade before the federal map, the Afro reported that in Waverly, 'where colored people have long lived, and built up churches,' white community associations were pressing Black residents to give up their homes and churches for the northwest section — while across town white residents blocked a Black congregation from buying a church. The private 'improvement-association' machinery the HOLC would later formalize in ink.

For 1937 booking agent Douglass O. Smith secured Oriole Park for the Elite Giants' night games, opening a park 'shut to colored teams for years.' Then it closed again: owner Tom Wilson wanted the park but balked at Smith's fee, and white residents complained to park officials about 'the noise and fanfare' of the night games. For 1938 the Elites were pushed to Bugle Field. The line was undone not by a rule but by a fee and a neighborhood's noise complaint — the same pretext used to evict the Elites for good in 1942.

The 1939 Elite Giants — with championship-series games played on this ground during the season — clinched the Negro National League title over the Homestead Grays. In the deciding game at Yankee Stadium, Sept 24, 1939, Jonas 'Lefty' Gaines shut out the Grays for seven innings and Baltimore won 2–0, taking the NNL championship and the Ruppert Cup — the best season in the franchise's Baltimore run, by a club shut out of the white ballpark's gate.

When Black world featherweight champion Chalky Wright defended his title at the park (stopping Baltimore's Harry Jeffra by TKO, Jun 19, 1942, before ~6,000), he carried a lineage: his grandfather, Caleb Baines Martin, was a runaway from a Natchez plantation who became a Buffalo Soldier and the first African-American ranch owner in southwest Arizona. The site's clearest world-championship night ran a bloodline from bondage to a title belt onto this ground.

Eighty-six years before the ballpark burned, another fire took the same corner. St. John's Episcopal — standing 'at the first toll-gate on the York road,' the exact spot where home plate would sit — was deliberately torched at 2 a.m.; the sacramental vessels stolen, the building gone before the companies arrived. 'The walls are of stone, and they are still good' — and the stone church survives today. Two fires, 86 years apart, on one tollgate corner (1858 arson; the July 4, 1944 ballpark blaze).

At Shiloh AME on E. 28th St., Richard L. Steiner of the Baltimore Redevelopment Commission told ~100 families they'd get 'a good price' for homes the city had claimed. The Waverly site — 17 acres bounded by Greenmount Ave., Reese St., 27th and 30th (taking in the ballpark parcel's own blocks) — was one of Baltimore's first two blighted-area clearance projects. Residents formed the interracial Waverly Area Association to protect themselves. The graded corridor 'cleared' acre by acre — the through-line from the 1937 map to the bulldozer.

A library due-date card from 'Young Actors' Workbook,' Roland Park Middle School: 'Tupac Shakur, class 8-15,' stamped Feb 20 & 27, 1985. Tupac spent his early years in Baltimore — Roland Park Middle, then the Baltimore School for the Arts, a short walk from the wedge — before the family left for California. Years before the voice, the artifact: a kid checking out an acting book a mile from the ballpark's ashes, the ground's Black-excellence lineage running from the Elite Giants and Chalky Wright into hip-hop's Baltimore roots.

The 1982 folder 'Waverly Harry's Facade and Logo' contains a full facade rendering for Harry's Liquors at 3113 Greenmount Avenue -- restored cornice, repaired brick, a coherent fascia sign -- plus a lettered sign-band study. A 'While You Were Out' telephone message slip preserved with the drawings records the delivery machinery: a contractor's list requested, a cost estimate from Bob Quilter, a storefront referenced. Design assistance, contractor brokering and cost estimating were a single workflow. A Harry's Liquors trades at the address today on an active licence, in a building whose retail lineage runs from Knoblock Brothers' grocery in the 1920s through leather goods by 1937 to liquor thereafter; the documentary chain for the trade name itself is continuous only from 2013, and the original Harry is unidentified. Box 10, folder 28.

The revitalization program resurfaced, striped, landscaped and lit the Waverly Shop & Park Lot at 3201 Barclay Street (Block 3881A, Lot 001), with design work in 1979-80 and construction in 1980-81, plus a dedicated expenditures file in 1980. The lot has a merchants' prehistory: a June 1958 'Park Free While You Shop' co-operative announcement listed some thirty-five participating stores and a new 32nd Street parking lot. The ground itself carries a buried history, having been the site of segregated Public School No. 115, in operation from 1889 until the 1950s and demolished in 1960. A deed recorded 30 November 1979 (WA 3844/396) falls inside the rebuild window and may record a city acquisition rather than an internal transfer. The lot remains city-owned and is operated today as the 'Waverly Lot.' Box 10 folders 24-26, 36; Box 10B folder 41.

The 32nd Street Farmers Market opened on 30 May 1980, conceived the previous year by a city housing employee who walked past the Waverly Shop & Park Lot while the revitalization program was rebuilding it. The market has operated continuously ever since, outlasting the Waverly Merchants Association, the urban renewal plan that authorised the lot's reconstruction, and every other institution involved in the 1976-1983 program. It is the most durable thing the Waverly System produced, and it was not in the plan.

George J. Bluso (1920-2009, buried Dulaney Valley Memorial Gardens, Timonium; wife Angelina 1924-2004) purchased 3223 Greenmount Avenue on 16 March 1977 and signed the July 1978 Waverly Merchants Association newsletter as president sixteen months later, announcing the city's commercial revitalization program and its capital schedule. He held the property into the 1990s. Newspaper research records a George J. Bluso of the same city with a 1953 gambling conviction (given as age 34, of the 5600 block Purdue Avenue), a September 1960 federal arrest for bookmaking without a federal gambling stamp, a May 1961 appearance in reporting on a case connected to an East Baltimore Street club (given as age 42, same Purdue Avenue address), a Baltimore Sun description in 1970 as 'a major gambling figure in the area' who served a year in 1964, and a reported federal decision vacating a wagering-tax conviction (Bluso v. United States, 375 F. Supp. 1085, D. Md. 1974). CAUTION: the two newspaper ages agree with each other at a birth of about 1918-19, while the memorial gives 1920; year-only memorial dates are frequently approximate, but the identification is NOT yet confirmed. The decisive test is the grantee clause of the 16 March 1977 deed (RHB 3457/824-830): if it names a grantee residing in the 5600 block of Purdue Avenue, the merchants' president and the gambling defendant are the same man.

Preservation documentation was not performed decades after the revitalization program as an unrelated exercise; it was intertwined with it. The Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation's City of Baltimore Neighborhood Survey covered Waverly in 1977, surveyed by Michelle Belco, generating Maryland Inventory of Historic Properties forms in a wave running roughly B-2776 to B-2817, with the Greenmount corridor's forms at B-2785 through B-2791. The DHCD program files carry a parallel 'Waverly Historic Survey' folder for 1977-1978, and a Maryland Historical Trust inventory form for 3021-3031 Greenmount Avenue citing the 1977 city survey was filed alongside the merchants' newsletter. The buildings' architectural character was becoming part of the district's economic strategy thirty-six years before the National Register district was listed.

The revitalization program's lending arm is documented on this block: in January 1980 the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, through the Department of Housing and Community Development, lent the Adlers $67,000 against 3220 Greenmount Avenue as a city rehabilitation loan, mid-program. A comparable stack appears one block north in December 1981, where a $75,000 City of Baltimore / DHCD loan combined with a $125,000 SBA loan was expressly 'applied to the rehabilitation of properties known as Nos. 3202-05-07-09 Greenmount Avenue' for the retail tenant The Princess Shops. Together these establish that the Commercial Revitalization Division's public money was rebuilding Greenmount retail blocks, not merely drawing them.

Every HOLC zone at the Waverly four-corners - A1 (Guilford), B16, C9, D6, and the ballpark's own C4 - was appraised by the same man on the same day: Louis Kroner, property review appraiser, H.O.L.C., May 4, 1937. His sheets (verbatim, Mapping Inequality transcriptions) span a sevenfold income gradient across ~150 m: A1 "Executives, Professional men," income "Over $5,000," Negro "No," trend upward, favorable influence "Close to business area on Greenmount Ave."; D6 "Laborers," income "$700-1,000," "Negro: Yes, 35" (35% foreign-born), "Houses in very bad condition. Many alley properties"; remarks "Vandalism in this section" - and, as D6's listed FAVORABLE influence: "Near desirable properties." C4 (the Oriole Park V ground): population "Mixture," income $2,000, favorable "Goucher college located in the section. Desirable location," detrimental "Industrial plants. Continuing obsolescence of old property," trend static. The four-corners was not four judgments that collided; it was one administrative act - executed three weeks after the ballpark's Negro National League opening day (April 10, 1937).

The Waverly study Survey Influence section quantified the survey itself as a market intervention, in the year ending June 1, 1940: HOLC loans repaid in full nearly doubled; borrowers in default dropped by more than half; for-sale signs fell about 50 percent and for-rent signs over 90 percent; HOLC sales of foreclosed Waverly properties jumped from 24 percent (prior three years) to 57 percent in one year - while Maryland overall FELL from 37 to 34 percent. The measurement was the medicine. The same chapter found definite evidence of overzoning on Greenmount Avenue between Thirty-fifth and Forty-second Streets (also Old York Rd 34th-35th and 33rd St), and recorded early Master Plan wins: the old junk yard and unsightly frame tabernacle at the NW corner of Venable Ave and Old York Rd removed and the lot paved; the first of 12 planned interior play areas (block 3903-A) approved by the Park Commission at 1,286.25 dollars - an assessment of 36.75 dollars per property.
